speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: RATIONING
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO DISTRIBUTION OF RATION BOOKS THROUGH LOCAL BOARDS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) on February 3 on the orders of the day asked a question about the distribution of ration books. I thought it would be much more convenient if I could table the answer, which I now do. It is as follows:
Under war conditions there has been tremendous movement of population. No agency who has tried to do so has ever been very successful in obtaining notification of changes of address. It is estimated that the post office, which one would expect to be in a very strong position, receives only about one-third of the address changes. There are numerous indications which point to the fact that the ration administration is not being notified of a great percentage of the address changes. When book No. 1 was distributed by mail the ration administration had a mailing list which was only three months old and which they had kept up to date by
Ration Books

making all changes of which they were * advised. Nevertheless in the city of Toronto alone, 62,000 of these books were returned to them. It was a most laborious process to get these into the proper hands and inevitably the book holders were greatly inconvenienced. In the six months which have elapsed since that date, additional address changes have accumulated. About half the population of the dominion has no street address. They collect their mail from rural routes or from general delivery.
The ration administration has available now an organization comprising local ration boards which form the basis for distribution. Volunteer workers have been enthusiastic in their offers to help and the ration administration expect the job to proceed with little inconvenience.
In spite of precautions taken, some persons have received two books. Worked out on a percentage basis, the number of these is small; however, they should be eliminated if possible. While some persons accept two books mailed to them at different addresses, it would be much less likely that they would deliberately present themselves twice to make applications.
Expense is also a factor of some importance. In order to distribute the ration books through the post office, millions of pieces of mail would have to be handled and the ration administration would be involved in considerable expense in readdressing books returned to them owing to change of address.
It is perhaps worth mentioning that the distribution of book No. 2 differs from that of book No. 1 by the fact that the former includes butter coupons which have an expiry date. When book No. 1 was distributed anyone who received his book a few weeks late at least had the satisfaction of knowing that he could still use all the coupons. With book No. 2 it would bo different to the extent that anyone receiving a book a few weeks late will have lost the opportunity of using some of the butter coupons.

maintopic: QUESTIONS

speechtext: What is the reason for Wartime Housing Limited not making provision to use part of the staff house at Peterborough for women?

maintopic: QUESTIONS
subtopic: WARTIME HOUSING-ACCOMMODATION FOR WOMEN IN PETERBOROUGH STAFF HOUSE
speechtext:
In October, 1941, following a survey of munition plants in Peterborough, it was recommended by the Department that two staff houses be erected in Peterborough

one for men and one for women. This was approved by P.C. 8874, dated November 18,

Questions
1941. It was felt that caution should be exercised in proceeding with two staff houses at one time. It was thought probable that the erection of one staff house might release enough accommodation in Peterborough to make the construction of a second one unnecessary. As the industries in Peterborough considered their first necessity to be housing accommodation for men, a men's staff house was first proceeded with.
Should it be that the condition arises whereby only one staff house be necessary to house both the men and women unable to be housed other than in staff houses, then the Peterborough staff house can, by minor and simple modification, be made to house both men and women workers. The Department of Munitions and Supply as a matter of principle is averse to housing men and women in the same building if it can be avoided. The department, at the present time, has no reason to believe that the present staff house will not be entirely required for men, and it has no advice that accommodation for women is presently needed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS
subtopic: THIRD VICTORY LOAN-COMMISSIONS TO BOND DEALERS
speechtext:
No commissions are paid to investment dealers on the sale of victory bonds. However, the Minister of Finance, on the recommendation of a committee consisting of the chairman of the national war finance committee, the securities adviser of the Bank of Canada, and the Deputy Minister of Finance, pays a reasonable remuneration to such dealers for the services rendered by them in connection with each victory loan campaign. The basis of this remuneration is not disclosed to dealers but takes into account the number and character of the personnel made available to the national war finance committee and the previous record of the firm in the distribution of dominion government securities. It is considered undesirable to disclose the amount paid to individual firms as to do so would divulge to competitors the business affairs of private firms and might adversely affect the morale of the victory loan organization.
The total amount of remuneration paid to investment dealers in Canada for services rendered in connection with the third victory loan was $3,067,415, or -309 per cent of the amount of money raised.

Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to be called the Supplementary 1942 War Appropriation Act to provide inter alia,
1.	That sums not exceeding $858,000,000 be granted to his majesty in addition to the sums granted by the War Appropriation Act, 1942, towards defraying any expenses or making any advances or loans that may be incurred or granted by or under the authority of the governor in council during the year ending March 31, 1943, for:
(a)	the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada;
(b)	the conduct of naval, military and air operations in or beyond Canada;
(c)	promoting the continuance of trade, industry and business communications, whether by means of insurance or indemnity against war risk or in any other manner whatsoever; and
'(d) the carrying out of any measure deemed necessary or advisable by the governor in council in consequence of the existence of a state of war.
2.	That the governor in council be empowered to reexpend, advance or loan moneys that may be received by way of refund or repayment of advances, loans or expenditures under the War Appropriation Act, 1939, the War Appropriation Act, 1940, the War Appropriation Act, 1941, the War Appropriation Act, No. 1, 1942, the AVar Appropriation Act, No. 2, 1942, and the Supplementary 1942 War Appropriation Act.
He said: I stated the other day, Mr. Speaker, that His Excellency the Governor General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the consideration of the house.

Mr. Speaker, before the house goes into committee, I am quite sure that the minister is prepared to make a statement supplementary to that already made.

War Appropriation

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am quite prepared to make a brief statement before we go into committee, although I have not prepared any statement. I am prepared, however, to answer questions. As I said the other day, I hope we shall be able to get this resolution through as soon as possible for the reasons I then gave.
This resolution is to provide for sums not exceeding 8858,000.000 to be granted to his majesty by way of supplementary war appropriation for the current fiscal year. The amount already voted is $2,000,000,000, and from the most careful estimates that can now be made it would appear that we shall need before the end of the current fiscal year another $858,000,000. If members are interested, the initial estimate of the last year will be found in the Hansard of March 17, 1942, at page 1531. The estimate there is for $2,213,000,000. It would have been more than that if it had not been anticipated that there was some duplication between the estimates of the Department of National Defence and the Department of Munitions and Supply. It would have been $2,363,000,000 but for that. It is therefore not correct to say that our war estimates have been exceeded or will be exceeded by $858,000,000 in the current fiscal year, because we did not ask the house to vote the total amount of our estimates last year. I explained then, I think, that it is impossible to forecast with any accuracy the demands which will be made upon the treasury in time of war. So much depends upon developments that one can only make an approximation. The practice that has been followed in the last two or three years has been this. I have brought before the house the estimates for the war departments and the war estimates for the other departments, which have added up to more than the amount I have asked the house to vote. That was the case last year. As it turns out I would have been safe in asking the house to vote more than our estimates last year instead of less, but having asked the house to vote less than $2,213,000,000 I have now to come and ask the house for *what appears to be a very large additional amount. SS58,000,000. There have been many unanticipated programmes and projects through the year and additions have been made from time to time to the war estimates. On the other hand, though I cannot give the house details at the moment, some of the projects which were anticipated have not made the demands upon the treasury that were expected or have not been carried out in the way that was expected. So that there
is a great lack of agreement between the amounts spent during the fiscal year in time of war and the amounts which it is anticipated at the beginning of the fiscal year will have to be spent.
I should say that during the summer and fall it was expected that our total expenditures would amount to about $3,900,000,000. That was the figure I gave in the budget last June and it is the figure I used whenever I was asked about the matter thereafter. Now it would appear, as I have stated recently, since the beginning of the year-I think, in the house; certainly outside the house, before the house met-that our total expenditure for the entire fiscal year will be nearer $4,500,000,000 than $3,900,000,000.

I am not an economist, but it was a surprise to me that the country was capable of such a large expenditure, that there would be goods and services available produced by the people of the Dominion of Canada to such a high amount. It shows how productive the country is, what a great capacity for production there is.
These are the fundamental facts underlying these estimates: that our expenditures will be about $4,500,000,000 during the fiscal year, instead of $3,900,000,000; and when it is borne in mind that we did not vote the full $3,900,000,000, it will be seen that what I am asking is substantially consistent with these figures.

speechtext:
The minister stated just now that he was amazed at the capacity of the Canadian people to rise to the position of production by which they are capable of handling as large a budget as that which the minister has just indicated. I think perhaps all of us are amazed at this. I might point out, however, to the minister and the government, and with this I will conclude, that all sections of the people are anxious that whatever is required to win this war shall be given-whether it be in man-power, in material, or in finance. That is a pledge to which our people have definitely committed themselves in order that this battle for freedom shall be won. But while they are willing to shoulder whatever financial burdens may be necessary that are within their power, they also expect that every dollar which is given to the government for this very important object shall be spent without waste and without inefficiency.
We hope that during this session, when the war appropriation bill is presented to the house, it will be presented in sufficient detail to enable members of the opposition and all other hon. members to have the opportunity of examining, perhaps more closely than has ever been done before, each of the details in connection with the war expenditures covered by these large amounts. To-day nearly every person in Canada, according to his or her ability, is required to pay; I think hon. members in general will corroborate my statement that more people at this time are conscious of government expenditures than ever were before, and that there is a growing desire among the ordinary taxpayers of the country that every dollar given by them to this worthy purpose shall be properly and effectively spent. I warn the government that we shall require the war appropriations to be set before us in greater detail than ever before. That, I believe, is in the interest of the people, and to insist upon anything less would not be to discharge properly our duties as members of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I do not propose to make a speech; I shall say only that in conformity with the understanding arrived at, we are prepared to allow this appropriation bill to go through as rapidly as possible. When we come to the main bill we should like a complete break-down of the expenditure over the current year so that we may understand precisely how the money has been spent.
It is an amazing thing to many people that Canada has been able to find the large amount of material supplies which is represented by

the sum of money involved. We may congratulate the Canadian people that the Canadian economy has been able to do this in war time; and if I may say so. I think our people expect that when the war is over we shall be able to find the same materia! things, and to the same or greater extent if necessary, for the building of this country in the postwar period. I look forward to seeing the government plans of the future for the construction of this country in the post-war period.
We shall, however, want to make a thorough inquiry into these expenditures when the main appropriation is before the house.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Members of the Social Credit party are desirous of enabling the government to expedite the passage of this bill. We realize that they require the money, and it is our desire to see that they have the money to fight the war.
I think it is timely that we point out to the minister that we are not surprised that he should have said he was amazed at the productive capacity of Canada. We are not at all surprised that the leaders of the Progressive Conservative and the Cooperative Commonwealth groups should have said the same thing. We wish to draw to the attention of hon. members the fact that in 1935 we social crediters began to point out that there was a tremendous productive capacity in Canada, and that Canada's productive power could be mobilized by a monetary technique. The members of the government were merely tolerantly indulgent of the foolish ideas which they thought we were expressing.
Canada had the same productive capacity in 1935 that she has to-day. But the powers in control did not see fit to allow Canada's productive capacity to be used and the result thereof to be distributed among the Canadian people to enhance their well-being. That could have been easily done, just as well as it can be done now.
I wish to point out one other matter that is vital in this connection. Even yet the members of the government and parliament generally have not come to recognize that all these vast wartime productive schemes could have been accomplished without increasing the debt in Canada. As has been pointed out time and again, what is physically possible is fiancially possible; where the productive capacity of Canada actually exists the financial capacity is there, and the end can be achieved without debt and without injurious taxation. May I point out to the government that one of the most, important

TTar Appropriation
tasks confronting the administration to-day, as it approaches a possible peace, is that of finding a means-some means must be discovered-whereby the productive capacity of Canada, as is evidenced by the tremendous achievement during this war, shall continue to be used after the war.
Production has been stimulated during the war by the borrowing and spending of money. Where productive capacity exists the money can be spent, and it need not be borrowed. It is the spending of money which causes inflation, if inflation is the result; it is not the place from which a government gets the money. State money, debt free, could have resulted in the same production, whether in peace or in war, as has been brought about by the means already used. The resultant production could have been distributed in time of peace among the people, if the government had had vision enough to see how the distribution of goods could be effected among the Canadian people.
To-day we are becoming fairly prosperous, or would be, if it were not for the scrupulous care with which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) through his taxation structure limits our prosperity. We are becoming prosperous because we are distributing our goods in the form of munitions and instruments of destruction abroad. In order to obtain the financial prosperity in Canada which results from the manufacturing of tanks Canada does not need to manufacture tanks and send them over to Hitler to be destroyed. The same prosperity could result from the manufacturing of anything to be used in Canada, the difference being that in the case of something to be used in Canada, Canada would have not only the money to spend here but the goods to use as well.
I do not wish to discuss this matter at any great length now but it seems fitting that the members of the house should be very thoughtful in view of the tremendous productive power which has been evident in Canada.
One thing more. Our productive capacity has not yet been fully exploited. Enormous quantities of additional foodstuffs of many kinds can be produced in Canada. Canada is capable of producing a tremendous quantity of rubber by synthetic processes, huge quantities of gasoline, great quantities of sugar and an abundance of fruit which we have not yet produced.

and if a financial technique wTere perfected whereby that could be brought about and the resulting goods distributed, all without taxation, we should then see the way to a new order in which the standard of living of the Canadian people would bear some sort of relation to their productive capacity.
We are prepared to cooperate with the government to the limit in providing the money to enable Canada to make the greatest war effort that it is possible for her to make, considering the man-power and other resources at her disposal.

speechtext:
I regret that the minister, in the course of the all too brief observations which he made with respect to this resolution, did not take occasion to give a break-down of the $858,000,000. On February 8, at page 217 of Hansard, he referred to the fact that funds for the transfer of munitions plants from the imperial government to the Canadian government would be requested in the supplementary war appropriation bill; but apart from that I can find very little reference to the items which are to be covered by this appropriation. There is of course reference to other matters which presumably may or may not be in the bill. I am going to ask the minister, at the conclusion of the brief remarks which I have to make, to give us a break-down of the whole sum of $858,000,000.
Having regard to the undertakings which were given by my leader and the leaders of the groups in the house, the discussion of (his matter must of necessity be very limited. Let me say at the outset that since the minister has made it clear that the money must be voted immediately, that it is a national necessity in order that the contractual obligations of the nation may be promptly met, there is no disposition on the part of anyone to hold up the bill. But I may say I was startled, as I think the country will be, at the size of this supplementary bill, having regard to what we were told during the last session of the house. Perhaps it would not be out of place if we were to have a review of the whole position. The minister expressed amazement that the people of Canada could sustain the weight of a war expenditure of the size and scope they are being asked to sustain. The answer is that this government is asking the people of Canada to bear a greater ratio of load in proportion to the national income than is the case in either of the other two large belligerent nations. I have before me a review contained in a federal
40S
War Appropriation

reserve publication issued just prior to January 15 which reveals that the proportion of the national income devoted to war purposes is considerably less in the United States than it is in either Great Britain or Canada. This bulletin shows that the war effort in the three countries is absorbing the national income according to the following percentages: United States, 24-5 per cent; Great Britain, 36-8 per cent, and Canada, 39-1 per cent. If these figures mean anything, and if I correctly interpret them, they show that the Canadian people are being asked by this government to contribute to the war effort a greater proportion of the national income than either our rich neighbours to the south or our very hard-pressed blood brothers overseas.

speechtext:
I do not quite see the relevancy of that remark. I may be dense, but I cannot correlate that suggestion with the point I am trying to make. I am speaking of the portion of the national income being taken by the government for war purposes from the people of Canada as compared with the portion taken by our neighbours to the south and our friends overseas. To me that means that the Canadian people are being taxed more heavily than are our friends in the United States or our friends in Britain, that we are asked to do more in terms of dollars and cents than either of those countries. I am assuming that these percentages are correct. I have no means of checking them, but since they are given out by the federal reserve system I assume at once that they are accurate.
That tells the story. It is often said in this house by certain parties that too much emphasis is being laid on the problem of man-power qua the army. I want to say that in my view -and I do not care who gets the credit or discredit, for that does not mean anything- this country is doing more financially than any other of the united nations. I am not complaining about that, but the question has arisen as to how far we may go in personal income taxes. I am reminded that last summer, during the course of a tour, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson) made the statement, if I remember correctly, that personal income taxes in this country had reached their peak. I understand that statement was not very pleasing to the members of the government at a later stage ,and perhaps the minister was a little indiscreet in making it. However, he did make it, and I presume he was speaking for the government.

That shows that the loyal people of this country are willing to pay to help win this war, as well as giving their sons and now their daughters in the national cause. Whoever says there is not conscription of wealth in this country by -way of taxation, no matter what may be the vehicle of taxation, just does not know what he is talking about and is talking very loosely. I wonder sometimes just how much farther we can go.
The size of this supplementary bill is astonishing. When the minister brought down war appropriation bill No. 1 for $2,000,000,000 he gave the estimates and asked for the round figure, and left his position open in regard to the estimates he gave. But I do not understand how they could vary so greatly. I do not understand how there could be such a wide variation between the estimates and the actual results. It is true that we have increased our armed forces and increased our production, but this is a very large sum. It may include some items of which I have no knowledge; from the remarks of the minister I think it does include an amount for the acquisition of war plants. How much that amounts to, I do not know; would it be $200,000,000?

speechtext:
Very well. I think therefore that as a duty to the people of Canada I should put on record a clear view of what is the position in dollars and cents, and to that end I have prepared as best I could a brief statement.
During the session of 1942, war appropriation bills No. 1, which I think was assented to on June 9, and No. 2, of which I have not the date of assent before me, provided for the sum of $2,000,000,000. In addition we had the United Kingdom war financing act, which appropriated another $1,000,000,000. Then wTe had the peace-time estimates amounting to $454,000,000 in round figures, and supplementary peace-time estimates of $28,000,000, making the total peace-time estimates $482,000,000. These three figures aggregate $3,482,000,000. Under this war-time supplementary resolution that we are being asked to consider for the present fiscal year the amount is $858,000,000, making a grand total of $4,340,000,000-a sizable sum for eleven and a half million people.
According to an answer brought down on Monday last to a question put by the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) which will be found on page 202 of Hansard, the latest published estimate of direct war expenditure for the present fiscal year ending March 31, 1943, including the gift to Britain, was $3,900,000,000. And the latest estimate

War Appropriation
for peace-time expenditure is $600,000,000. I understand how the $3,900,000,000 is made up, but I am at a loss to account for the difference between $482,000,00 peace-time main estimates plus supplementaries and this estimate of $600,000,000. a difference of $118,000,000. I think the Canadian people will require some explanation from the minister at a suitable time as to why our peace-time estimates so far exceed the amount of the vote of this house.
The peace-time estimates should be reduced instead of increased. The government made some show of endeavouring to decrease them; witness the appointment of Mr. John Thompson. I do not know how far he will get. I know that there was a very limiting factor in the order in council appointing him; I understand that has been amended so that now he has full authority to go into every department, which authority was at first denied him. But the minister ought to give some explanation in regard to that $118,000,000 excess in the peace-time estimates. It will be rather a shock to the people of Canada to learn of that. While we exceed the war-time estimates by many millions of dollars and might reasonably expect that, to have also SllS.000,000 of peace-time expenditure beyond what we were told at the last session of parliament is something I do not understand. There will have to be some explaining to the Canadian people as to why we have exceeded or are about to exceed our estimated peacetime expenditures to the extent of $118,000,000. I have a suspicion that a very large portion of expenditures which might properly be charged to peace-time activities is included in the war appropriation bill and paid out of that fund. We have not much to say about the distribution; we know about it only after the event. But if that suspicion is well founded-I am only calling it a suspicion, because I have not the time or the ability to dig it out myself, neither have I the information available

I would assume that a very large sum of peace-time expenditure is included in the war appropriations, and that if the real truth were passed on to the people of Canada we should find the peace-time activity expanded not merely to $600,000,000 this year instead of $482,000,000, but to a substantially larger sum than that.
Now according to the same answer, the revenues from all sources for the fiscal year ending March 31 next are estimated at $2,250,000,000. Having regard to the greatly increased rates of taxation, this estimate is probably accurate. No doubt the officials of the Department of Finance have made a careful estimate as to what the probable
revenues are from the returns already available and from the flow of funds to the treasury.
From these figures I draw two inferences: first, that there has not been very careful planning by the government with respect to war financial expenditures. As a matter of fact one of the charges against the government is that there has been no all-out planning of our war effort, in relation not only to this, but also to nearly every other activity. Certainly that is true with respect to the man-power situation, about which I hope to have something to say on a later occasion. Yet here we are to-day in the position that the cupboard is bare, the treasury depleted, because of what I call a lack of planning on the part of the administration. All the greatly increased revenues, the proceeds of the huge loans subscribed by the Canadian people, are gone, or nearly so. I think an explanation is due to the Canadian people far beyond that which the minister gave this afternoon. We all assumed that there would be some supplementary war appropriation bill for this fiscal year, but I do not think any of us every visualized a bill to the extent of $858,000,000.
The second lesson I draw-and I hope I am wrong-is that there has been some lack of treasury control over expenditures. In the course of this discussion the minister should tell us just what the treasury control is over war expenditure as well as over peace expenditure. The minister is very alert to tax the people; no one can accuse him of lack of initiative in levying taxes. I have heard him many a time urge them to tighten their belts and to lend and give to the utmost. So far as I am concerned I have had to tighten my belt; I can speak from personal experience. But I am not complaining-I am not in a position to do very much else- although I have found it very hard going, as many another has. I am willing to pay, because I cannot contribute much otherwise. But I wonder whether the minister is just as alert in protecting the public in connection with these war-time expenditures as he is in getting the money to make them.
Time was when the minister of finance was the guardian of the public treasury. I put this query to him: How far has that function been performed? What about extravagant expenditures and waste? Probably the minister will challenge me, as I was challenged last year, to name them, and on the spur of the moment I said: Look around you. Some newspaper supporting the government said I was referring to the number of page boys in this house. Of course I was not
War Appropriation

referring to anything of the sort. But if the minister wants an answer I refer him to the speech made last year by his follower the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. McLean), to which the government has given heed in connection with expenditures in the operation of this House of Commons. That speech did a lot of good, and the preparation of it must have taken a great deal of time. But if you will look around in this country, if you will listen to what the public are saying, you will realize that they are condemning this government for the waste that is going on everywhere. I have evidence that orders have gone out in the army to prevent waste, and that is all to the good. But it is in response to public opinion. Things have been tightened up in the training camps, for instance, and expenditures are being restricted. That was not always so. It certainly was not so with the Minister of National Defence for Air, who was very disarming on one occasion when he told us that speed was the only consideration. He so disarmed me that I could not go on and criticize him.

when you cannot do that; I know there are conditions under which it is not possible, but the competitive system has much merit.

I could give a number of instances, but I shall refer only to one, the prices paid for land in connection with the Gimli airport. I do not say that there was any graft in connection with it; I do not know anything about it, but a newspaper in Winnipeg made an examination and came to the conclusion that two or three times as much was paid for submarginal land in that district as should have been paid. speechtext:
Why the
dyke? I have lived on the marshes of Westmorland county and I know why the dykes are there. They are put there to protect against inundation by the sea. I am not going any further into this sort of thing, but I do want to impress upon the minister the necessity of treasury control. I know there are many people who will say that the expenditures of the army must not be interfered with by the treasury, but I say to the army that treasury control is absolutely necessary; the civil authority must at all times be paramount over the military authority in any democracy.	.
We are willing to vote for this measure in order that the national honour may be maintained, but I warn the minister that the country is expecting much from him by way of protection against waste. Last year, the

TFar Appropriation
year before and the year before that I said that the people of Canada from the highest to the lowest would give gladly and willingly according to their ability to give and pay, but they would expect a dollar's worth of value for every dollar of expenditure. They would expect all waste to be eliminated and they would expect the government to watch expenditures. I repeat that to-day.
There are some other remarks that I desire to make in connection with this matter. We are told in the press that we are to have a national budget well in excess of $5,000,000,000 or perhaps $5,500,000,000. I have in front of me a Canadian Press dispatch from Ottawa, the heading of which states that the war is costing close to $6,000,000 daily and that Canada's expenditures for ten months had been $1,826,000,000, the average for January being $5,96S,000 daily. The item then goes on to say that in all probability we will have a budget in excess of $5,000,000,000 and perhaps $5,500,000,000.
What does that mean? It means a per capita expenditure of $500 for every man, woman and child in Canada. If we are to be called upon for that, it is the duty of the government to see that every dollar is properly expended. I must say that an anticipated budget of $5,500,000,000 for 11,500,000 people is something to cause us to think and think violent!}'. I am willing to pay the shot so far as my part of it is concerned, and I think all loyal citizens in Canada are willing to pay theirs, but I do not believe we ought to be asked to pay beyond our ability to pay. We should not be asked to pay a greater portion of the national income than the people are being asked to pay in hard-pressed Britain.
We shall vote for this resolution and the bill which will be based upon it, but I fear that the undertaking to provide an opportunity for full discussion of this $850,000,000 when the war appropriation bill comes on will not be very effective. We will be so concerned with an examination of the details of the huge war appropriation bill that this relatively trivial item of $858,000,000 will be lost sight of. I think the government should have brought down this bill a week ago. They should have suspended the debate on the address and given us a break-down of this sum so that we could have had time to consider it. The Prime Minister should have suspended the current business of the house if this bill was so urgent and we had to have this money as of to-day.
I want to repeat what my leader has said, that we reserve the right to investigate on a later appropriate occasion the whole breakdown of this $858,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think there will be any difficulty about examining the expenditures for the current fiscal year when the main appropriation bill is before the house, because that is the time when the ministers give an account of their activities over the past year. It is incidental to the passing of the new estimates that the various ministers concerned should rise in their places and state what has been spent and what has been done. As a matter of fact most of the discussion on the main appropriation bill is a discussion of what has been done, not of what will be done, and therefore the hon. gentleman need have no fear that there will be any skimping of discussion on these estimates.
Before I sit down I shall put on Hansard a break-down of the $S58,000.000. and for the convenience of members I will give them the citations from Hansard of last year, so that at their leisure-I hope they will not do it this afternoon or ask that this go over until to-morrow to enable them to do it-they can, before the main bill comes down, ascertain where the increases have been. It will be fairly clear, if they will look at Hansard of March 17, 1942. page 1531, which I cited before, and Hansard of June 1, 1942, page 3180, where a break-down of all expenditures of non-war departments is to be found, just what has been done. It may be that there are other pages of Hansard of last year where a break-down is given of the estimates of the war departments. I think there are, but I have not them before me. At any rate these two citations will give a very good idea where the increases have taken place. But before I give these figures I want to refer to two or three points made by my hon. friend.
The hon. gentleman spoke about the increase in the non-war expenditures from an estimate of $482,000,000 to an estimate now of $600,000,000. I am afraid that I cannot give him a final or complete and satisfactory explanation of that. I think, however, the explanation is this, that payments to the provinces and the increased interest on the debt account for the whole thing and more. It must be remembered that the interest on the debt which is in substance a war expenditure, is included in the non-war estimates. The hon. gentleman said that there was a tendency to charge to war what should be charged to peace. I think there is an inherent tendency, a natural tendency on the part of departments to do that, but it is a tendency which is combated by the treasury very resolutely, and, I believe, fairly successfully. If one goes through the
War Appropriation

amounts which have been charged to war I do not think there will be found in them anything that should not be charged to war.
Mr. HANSON- (York-Sunbury): In connection with the payment of subsidies, was there not a vote in the peace-time estimates of last year to take care of them?

speechtext:
There is no looseness or
laxity whatsoever in that regard. In explanation of that increase there is an important fundamental which anyone will understand when I put the facts before the house.
With regard to the proportion of our national income that we are spending on war as compared with Great Britain, I have been advised all along that we were not quite up to Great Britain, that we were not spending quite as large a proportion of our national income on war as they are doing in Great Britain. The figures which the hon. gentleman has given, while issued by a most respectable authority, may not be correct. I assume that they have taken some estimate of Canada's national income which may or may not be an accurate estimate. Any statement of Canada's national income is an estimate. I have read articles in the London Economist criticizing our estimates of our national income as being away too low. They may be; I do not know about that. It may be that the federal reserve board, if that was the authority that issued the statement, has used an estimate of our national income which is considerably too low. If so, the actual figures might show that the comparison was in favour of Great Britain rather than in favour of Canada. But if it is correct that we are spending a larger proportion of our national income on war than is Great Britain, that does away with the criticism that we are not conducting an all-out war effort, which has been the criticism of the government for the last two or three years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subsubtopic: SUPPLEMENTARY PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Finance is merely a measure, merely an index of what the people themselves are doing. That is all it is. When we talk about a certain proportion of the national income being devoted to war, all it means is that a certain proportion of the work that is done by the Canadian people, a certain proportion of the human and material resources of this countiy, is devoted to war. That is all it means, and the proportion of the national income in dollars that is devoted to war is merely an indication of the other.
With regard to United States, I would assume it is true that the United States is devoting a smaller proportion of its national income to war than is the Dominion of Canada, but the Dominion of Canada has been in the war since September, 1939, whereas the United States has been in the war only since December, 1941, and they have not yet by any means speeded up their activities to full capacity. If, however, they spend what the president says they will spend this year, they will spend much more than the Dominion of Canada proposes to spend in proportion to national income.
The hon. gentleman also said that the fact that these estimates have been so substantially exceeded is an indication that there has not been very careful planning. The planning was careful enough, but conditions have changed to such an extent. In May or June we revised the British commonwealth air training plan drastically, extending it widely to take effect the 1st of July. Situations also arose which required us to embark upon construction programmes of the most vital character, and our plans had to be altered. In fact, war plans are under a continual process of week by week alteration, and it is not a valid criticism to say that there is evidence of lack of careful planning because one changes one's programme during the course of the war, abandoning some parts and taking on other projects which are more expensive than the ones which have been abandoned.
Then the hon. gentleman said that there was a lack of treasury control. Well, we have in this country six thousand treasury officials. They are in all the departments. They are headed by the comptroller of the treasury; they make reports for me from time to time of anything they feel should be investigated. Members of the public send in criticisms of what they allege to be wasteful and extravagant expenditure; when they do, I write to the department and the minister inquires into it. If there is anything really wrong the practice is changed, and if there is not anything really wrong I send an explanation back to the person who wrote in. That, I think, is about the most the Department of Finance

War Appropriation
can. do. It is becoming almost impossible to get qualified auditors, cost accountants and so forth. As I said, we have already a staff enormously greater than before the war. We have our check when we pass the non-war estimates; we have our check when we pass the war estimates, and then we have the check on the expenditures which is provided by the officers of the comptroller of the treasury.

In a war effort of the dimensions of ours it is inevitable that here and there persons will be selected for positions of responsibility who have not the necessary qualifications for discharging those responsibilities. In other words, there will be some mistakes made. This happens in private business; it happens in every line of human activity. As long as the authority in charge-in this instance the government-has the right principle in regard to it, follows it up, and does not condone anything of the kind, that is about the best it can do. I know somebody may say that this sounds complacent, that we should go further.

Before submitting my remarks
on this resolution I should like to make a comment on what was said by the Minister of Finance a few minutes ago when he denied the statement made by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), that the Canadian people were more highly taxed than people in Britain or in the United States. The minister's statement may be correct to a certain extent, but I think he disregards the fact that our system of administration is different from that of England, where almost all taxes are collected by the central government. In Canada there are more taxing authorities, the provincial, municipal, school commissions and so on, and when all these taxes are added together it brings the figures above those paid by the people of Great Britain or of the United States.
I am also of opinion that an expenditure to the extent of nearly a billion dollars in excess of that authorized by parliament is not a habit that should be approved. In the years prior to the war parliament used to be convened to discuss budgets running about $400,000,000 or $450,000,000. It was right to do it. But this deficit alone is $858,000,000, or twice as much as we used to vote for an entire year prior to the war. And this was done while parliament was in session, because it was only adjourned. It would not have cost much to convene parliament and ask for further credit so that we could have studied where the money goes. For instance, I understand from paragraph 2 of the resolution and from what has been said and by the figures given by the minister a moment ago, that some of that money is to pay for goods which have been given to Great Britain on the same system as the billion dollar gift which we authorized last year. Such a transaction I do not think can be carried out without being authorized by parliament.
I recall seeing a few days ago a complaint by people in Australia that England had sold back to Australia goods which were given to her by th;s country. If people in this country are paying more taxes than people in Great Britain and the United States I do not think we have a right to give our goods to a country that is selling them. We are opposed to this resolution. It is a simple principle of business that we should sell those goods the same as England did; though it has not cost that country any sacrifice to produce goods, it cost our country heavy sacrifices to produce them. We are not able to do as much for the war, in which we are not as closely concerned as are Great Britain and the United States. We are not supposed to make the *war effort that those populations are compelled to make. We are a young country. For these reasons I am not going to support this -bill if it involves the payment for goods which have been granted by us to England, and which England has sold to another country, while some of those goods have been given without being authorized. The War Appropriation Act of last year providing for that gift to England was definite, and the government have not the right to go beyond it and give more than was authorized. For that reason I am going to oppose the resolution.

I want to correct the hon. gentleman. There is nothing in these estimates that provides for further gifts or further contributions. The war plants to which he refers constitute a different type of transaction. That is a case where we are obtaining title to plants in return for the money mentioned here.

War Appropriation

namely, 8200,000,000. The authority for making contributions to the United Kingdom was contained in the War Appropriation United Kingdom Financing Act, not in the ordinary War Appropriation Act and not in this supplementary War Appropriation Act. It is under a different act, it is a different type of transaction from anything provided for here. I want to put my hon. friend right on that point.
I want to put my hon. friend right on another point if I can. This is very hard to explain, hard not only for my hon. friend but for a great many members of the house to understand. If under the War Appropriation United Kingdom Financing Act we had sold our goods to Great Britain instead of giving them-he advocates selling them

our taxes would have been just as high and our borrowings just as great. I want to make that very clear, because many hon. members do not believe that, and a great many people in the country do not believe it. The only way in which we can reduce our tax burden or the amounts we borrow from the Canadian people would be by producing less, by putting less into the war effort, going easier, slackening, sagging back; that is the only way. Provided we go all out, do everything we can, make the goods and shells that are required, our tax burden is going to be there. The only effect of selling that stuff instead of giving it would be that we would have a cash drawer full of
1.0.	U.'s. The question is, do you want the
1.0.	U.s? Hon. gentlemen may think that if we had the I.O.U.'s it would in some way relieve the tax burden. But it would not. It is not Canadian dollars we get, because there are no Canadian dollars to get; it would be an obligation in the currency of another country we would have, not dollars at all. I wish hon. members would address their minds pointedly to that question and would not say, as some hon. members do, as one hon. member, the other night, in a debate to which I cannot under the rules refer, said, that we are taxing ourselves to provide money to give to another country. But that simply is not so. I repeat, our taxes are no higher than they would be if we were selling the stuff instead of giving it.
Then it is a question of how we want to finance. Some might say, well; do not take
1.0.	U.'s; do not take sterling; do not have your cash drawer full of sterling; but exact securities; strip Great Britain of any securities she has. That sounds plausible. But what would we do with the securities? If we sold $500,000,000 worth of securities to the Canadian people, our sale of victory bonds would be decreased by $500,000,000. We would not have

any more money in the treasury if we dfd that. It is true that the Canadian people instead of the British people would be holding the securities; but if we carry that process too far, and we have carried it a very long distance to date because we have expropriated $700,000,000 or $800,000,000 worth of securities, we imperil our post-war trading position. We shall be giving the British the strongest possible incentive to buy their wheat from the Argentine instead of from Canada. We shall be giving them the strongest incentive to deal with those people whose currency they have and not with Canada, of whose currency we have stripped them. We must be careful about that. We think our policy has been not only broad-minded but in our own interests. I implore hon. members not to say that we are taxing ourselves in order to raise money to give away-we are not.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the debate last Friday I intimated that there were two matters which I wished to lay before the house at this time, both referring to the income tax act. I am bringing these before the house at this time because I know the minister is working on his budget, and I want to direct his attention to them. I want to cite certain injustices in the hope that they will receive serious consideration by the minister and that an attempt will be made to remedy these grievances.
The matter to which I now wish to direct attention is the taxation as income of capital used in the production of oil and the development of the Turner valley oil field in Alberta. [DOT] At the outset let me make it clear that I am not quarrelling with the taxation of profits under the income tax act. What I do object to is the taxation as income of capital, capital that has been invested by the people in this country in the Turner valley oil field.
It takes about $225,000 to drill a well in Turner valley and to get production from the well. In the first place you have to pay the geologist. Then you have to purchase the oil lease, create and organize a company, sell royalties or shares to the amount of $150,000 or $175,000 to pay for the cost of drilling a well. You have to pay for surface rights, pay for roads, pay for drilling the well, pay royalties to the government, pay pipeline charges, municipal and school taxes, purchase production equipment, pay production costs, government taxes, conservation board assessment and office and general expenses. All of these items come to something like $225,000.
The life of a well when drilled is not long. You get the greatest production from an oil well when oil is first struck. During the first year you get a comparatively big production. During the second year you get much less, and by the end of the fourth or fifth or sixth year the production is so small that it is no longer profitable to operate the well.
The people who invest their money in drilling a well consider that they should be entitled to get back the money they have invested in the well. The government does

The Address-Mr. Ross (Calgary)
make provision to some extent for amortization, depletion and depreciation costs, but these costs are not allowed to be written off fast enough.
The instructions sent to the inspectors of income tax by the department are in part as follows:
The actual cost of pre-production development, including casing (exclusive of the cost of property and surface equipment) shall be allowed on the following basis:
1st year, 30 per cent of cost
2nd year, 20 per cent of cost
3rd year, 15 per cent of cost
4th yeax-, 12 per cent of cost
5th year, 10 per cent of cost
Thereafter 10 per cent until cost fully amortized.
Depletion will be allowed at 25 per cent of net profits from production after allowance of development charges and depreciation.
When a company starts out to drill a well no one can tell in advance what there is in the bowels of the earth. You may drill down to eight or nine thousand feet and get a "duster", a dry well. In that case no investor gets any of his money back. Or you may get a well producing two hundred barrels a day, and from such a well an investor can count on getting about one-third of his investment back, the balance being taken in taxes. You may strike a well which has an initial production- and it is initial production of which I am speaking-of four hundred barrels a day. In that event the investor may get two-thirds of his money back. The remainder is taken in taxes. A production of four hundred barrels a day is about what one can expect from the average well in Turner valley.
I suggest that this is unfair, unjust taxation. When the government revised the tax schedules last year the Oil Bulletin, an oil publication, called in a chartered accountant, a well-known authority on taxation, to make a study of the taxation situation. In his report as summed up by the editor of the Oil Bulletin this chartered accountant found:
(1)	Wells with initial oil flows of two hundred barrels per day would, during their productive life, fall short by between $170,000 and $195,000 of returning the cost of development (some $225,000);
(2)	Wells with initial flows of four hundred barrels per day (the approximate field average initial) would fall short by anything from $54,000 to $133,000 of returning costs.
In brief, under existing tax schedules, no investor can hope to recover his original stake from Turner valley wells in the "average" and "below average" groups; he has a chance of getting his money back with perhaps a very small profit from wells in the "above average" group; and, if his well is fortunate in being one of the big wells with initial allowable of eight Ixundred barrels daily, he may make a fair profit on his investment.

That is the finding of the chartered accountant who was engaged to investigate this matter.
I wish to read an editorial dealing with this matter which appeared in the Calgary Herald of February 5. It says:
Under the present income tax regulations, a Turner valley well has to produce six hundred barrels of oil a day or more to be a profitable investment. There are not many of them.
It is not surprising that under present conditions private investors are not keen to help finance well drilling programmes. If income tax concessions were granted, however, and the field price of crude oil were increased to a proper level, money would again be available for drilling purposes and thus maintain or increase production at a time when oil is vitally required by Canada.
At present the oil situation in Turner valley is desperate. Many rigs are idle. I am informed that there are twenty wells drilling at the present time as compared with thirty a year ago. The oil field is being taxed out of activity.
I suggest to the minister that it will be much better for everybody if this industry is allowed to survive. It will be better for the war effort, because we need the oil. It will be better for the government, because if they kill off the industry they cannot get taxes; if they allow the industry to live, a reasonable revenue can be obtained from it. It will be better for labour. It will also be better for investment, because a depressed industry will be built up and conditions in that area improved.
An order in council was recently passed, effective February 1, 1943, exempting from the war exchange tax and the tariff-
All machinery and apparatus and parts thereof (including motive power and rope) for use exclusively in exploratory or discovery work in connection with, and development, depletion and production of petroleum, natural gas or water wells, or in prospecting for minerals; seamless, lapwelded and electric welded iron or steel casing, tubing and drill pipe for use in connection with water, natural gas or oil wells.
That is very fine as far as it goes, but I should like to have seen it go much further, and extended to the machinery which is necessary in order to separate the oil and gas which come from the well, and the machinery which separates the oil from various impurities, in order to enable something to be done in the way of refining the oil. If, however, the industry i3 to be allowed to live, the change made will be helpful and will be much appreciated by 'the industry.

War Appropriation
A word with regard to prices. An article appeared recently in Maclean's magazine, reading in part as follows:
It is reported that the war transportation costs of bringing crude oil up the Atlantic seaboard are so high that the gross subsidy being paid by the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation is running at the rate of about fourteen cents a gallon.
There are thirty-five gallons of crude oil to a barrel, which means that a subsidy of $4.90 a barrel is being paid by the government. The Alberta operator is entitled to charge only one and a half dollars a barrel at the well head for his oil. Why is the government paying such a big subsidy for bringing in oil from the United States, and yet refusing, to allow our operators to charge more than $1.50 a barrel for oil at the well head? I cannot understand it. If there is any reason, I hope the minister will give it to us. It seems to me that the government could help the industry a great deal by increasing to some extent the price of oil there.
During last session I urged very strongly upon the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) and upon this house that there should be a ceiling on oil leases. I wish now to bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley), particularly, in the hope that he will place a ceiling on oil leases. Prior to the outbreak of the war ten per cent was the highest royalty ever charged by any government in Canada on oil leases. If governments could get along without it before the war I submit they should get along without it now, in view of the urgent need for oil at the present time. But, someone may say, the government of Alberta is only attempting to impose an additional royalty of two and a half per cent on all oil leases, and that is not very much. However, I wish to point out that that two and a half per cent is on gross royalties, and it means a tax of about ten per cent on net royalties, so that it is a considerable burden.
I do not believe there is another industry in Canada which is used so badly at the present time as the oil industry in Alberta.
