subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne emphasizes the greatly improved situation of the allied nations to-day as compared with a year ago. While the road to victory still may be a long, hard and rough one, nevertheless there need no longer be any doubt in the minds of the Canadian people as to our ability to achieve a final and decisive victory. However, it is essential for us to remember that winning this war is merely the first objective, the final objective being the making of a world peace under which it will be possible to bring to all people the greatest degree of economic and social security. It is well to remember that the soldiers of the last war made a very fine job of winning it, but that our statesmen and politicians made a ghastly failure of winning a peace that had any permanency attached to it.
If Canada is to play her part in helping to bring about that sort of peace, it is high time she put her own house in order. How can Canada be in a position to advise as to methods to bring about social security when she has failed so miserably in the past to provide that security for her own people? The speech from the throne lays a good deal of emphasis upon the need of guaranteeing to the peoples of the world freedom from fear and want. It is interesting to note that the speech from the throne of 1919 also laid a good deal of stress upon the need for the introduction of measures to provide for the welfare of the people. That speech reads as follows:
Further important measures, designed to promote the welfare and prosperity of the people in the new era of reconstruction, social as well as material, upon which the world has entered, will be recommended to your consideration.

The Address-Mr. Quelch
I note further that the speeches of the mover and the seconder of the address on that occasion also dealt with the need for the introduction of measures looking to the welfare and prosperity of the people. We know to-day how miserably those measures failed to bring about that sort of security. Have we any reason to-day to have any greater faith in the promises that are being made at this time with regard to post-war reconstruction? I suppose some people may feel a certain amount of confidence in the ability of the government to provide that security, as a result of the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) before the Canadian federation of labour on October 9 last, when he said:
Fortunately, we are also learning that the only limit to our productive capacity is the limit of our resources, and our will _ and skill to use them to satisfy human need instead of human greed.
Apparently the Prime Minister has a new vision in this regard. Is it not strange, however, that he had to be in power for twenty years before realizing the truth of that somewhat elementary, though fundamental principle? We emphasized that fact consistently from 1935 to 1939 and were ridiculed for our pains. The interesting point to note, however, is that this is not a new principle. Its soundness was recognized from 1914 to 1919. We never could have won the last war if we had not recognized the truth of that statement. I recall David Lloyd George saying that all the money needed in order to fight that war would be found. He pointed out that wars were not lost through lack of money but only through lack of ability to produce. Then in 1919 Mr. Lloyd George, during the course of a speech regarding the promise of a new world, showed only too clearly that he recognized the soundness of that principle. I quote from a report of that speech which appeared in the Western Producer of January 7:
Millions of gallant young men have fought for the new world, hundreds of thousands died to establish it. If we fail to honour the promise given them, we dishonour ourselves. What does a new world mean? What was the old *world like? It was a world where toil for myriads of honest workers, men and women, purchased nothing better than squalour, penury, anxiety and wretchedness-a world scarred by slums and disgraced by sweating, where unemployment through the vicissitudes of industry brought despair, to multitudes of humble homes; a world where, side by side with want, there was waste of the inexhaustible riches of the earth, partly through ignorance and want of forethought, partly through entrenched selfishness. If we renew the lease of that world we shall betray the heroic dead. We shall be guilty of the basest perfidy that ever blackened a people's fame.
I wonder if anyone would dare to say that the Right Hon. David Lloyd George was any
less sincere when he made that statement in 1919 than the Prime Minister to-day when he talks about a new social order. Some might say, Yes, but we have had a severe depression since that time. But that statement of David Lloyd George shows that there were severe depressions before. Yet we know that according to his own words we have been guilty of the basest perfidy, because there has been unemployment and abject misery throughout this country.
It was undoubtedly the will of the majority of the people of Canada from 1935 to 1939 that better conditions should be brought about. Then what was it that thwarted the will of the people in a so-called democracy? I would say that the reason why the people were not able to achieve the results they wanted was on account of the fact that in the past we have not had a real, live functioning democracy. It is true we have had political democracy; that is to say we have given the people voting power, but we have not given them a similar degree of economic power. And political democracy without economic power is democracy in name only. '
Let me try to explain what I mean by that statement. Democracy is largely a matter of degree, the degree to which the will of the people becomes supreme. Furthermore, the representative principle belongs to the very being of democracy. Then what are the checks on representative government that have in the past thwarted the will of the majority of the people? I would name three main checks: first, the constitution, second, the upper house, and, third, the direct intervention of the people. Of those three I would say the last is the only legitimate check on representative government.
The constitution I take first. I think we may say that where anything greater than a majority vote is required in order to amend a constitution, the will of a minority is enthroned. In many countries it takes two-thirds or three-quarters or even a one hundred per cent vote to change the constitution. When that is so you are allowing less than twenty-five per cent of the people to set aside the will of the majority. I believe ways and means will have to be found whereby an amendment of the constitution can be facilitated when the constitution stands in the way of the demands of the majority of the people. In that regard, however, I appreciate only too well that on various occasions the constitution has been used as an excuse for not bringing in social legislation that could have been introduced in spite of the constitution. In that regard I have in mind the old age pension. We could easily increase the old age pension to
424 '
The Address-Mr. Quelch

thirty dollars a month provided the federal government would assume the responsibility of financing it.
The second check to which I wish to refer is the upper house. In that regard we have two extremes in different countries. In some both houses are elected by the people, and in others one house is elected and the other appointed. In the United States and the U.S.S.R. both houses are elected; in Canada and Great Britain the House of Commons is elected and the other appointed. It is undoubtedly true that where you have a body of men who have been appointed and given the power to set aside the will of the people as expressed by the members who represent them, you have a distinct weakening of democracy. I believe that the upper chamber has long outlived its usefulness and could veiy well be abolished. To people who say these men are getting on in age and need some financial consideration I would reply that they should be given the same consideration as we give other aged people, namely the old age pension.
The third check is intervention by the electorate; that is the right of the people periodically to change their government. Yet it is a strange thing that in spite of the fact that the people have that power we have not enthroned the will of the people. Let me examine that for a few minutes.
The party system is, I think, possible only in a political democracy. It is not possible in a totalitarian state. The party system itself should be the guarantor of economic democracy. The system was evolved as a protest against special privilege; yet strangely enough to-day we find that the two old-line parties have to a large extent become servants of the very people who benefit by special privilege. In the past the main difference between the two old-line parties was the tariff. I wonder whether any hon. member could give any clear definition of the difference between the old-line parties of to-day. I think it was the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) who stated that the pnly difference is that one is in and the other is out; in other words, the difference between Tweedledum and Tweedledee. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer) in June, 1938, gave a very clear picture of the situation when he said he never thought it would be his misfortune to sit in a House of Commons where the leader of the opposition was more liberal than some Liberals sitting on the treasury benches. If I had been saying it I would have said, where some Liberals sitting on the treasury benches were more conservative than the leader of the opposition. Both statements
lMr. Quelch.]
mean the same thing. That statement was true in 1938. I believe it is even more true to-day.
When the two main political parties have no clear line of demarcation the result is bound to be a thwarting of the will of the people, because the people have no alternative vote. The result is that multiple parties come into existence, as we have them to-day. Real democracy, embodying economic as well as political democracy, is impossible under the two old parties as they exist to-day. I say that for this reason. Both parties are to a very large extent financed by the same interests. The people become befuddled by the party press and misguided by the independent press-independent only so far as party is concerned, not independent as far as their source of revenue is concerned. Multiple parties are therefore necessary in order to give expression to the progressive-minded people throughout the country. But I believe that the time is rapidly approaching in this country when there will be a realignment of the two main political parties of this country, a realignment representing two distinct ideologies. On the one side there will be those who believe in complete freedom of individual enterprise, rugged individualism, hands-off by the state, survival of the fittest; in other words, those who believe in a type of jungle law. On the other hand there will be those people who believe in a greater degree of intervention by the state in order to protect the people against exploitation by ruthless individuals and corporations. There you have two distinct policies leading to two distinct objectives.
In the first group would be what one might call the Conservative Liberal party, and in that party there will be those people who believe that the prosperity of a nation is to be judged by the size of the profits and dividends of the various corporations. It will be remembered that this is the definition which was given by a former Minster of Finance, Hon. Charles Dunning, in his budget speech in 1937. He pointed out at that time that Canada had reached an era of prosperity, and he said he based that statement upon the fact that the profits and dividends of various corporations had reached a new high level. He said that this was the only true criterion upon which one could base the prosperity of a nation.
In the second group there would be those who are socialistically minded, those who believe that the prosperity of a nation is to be judged by the general level of the wellbeing of the people and who adoveate a sufficient degree of government intervention to

The Address-Mr. Quelch
provide that type of security. I believe that this division will come in the very near future, that it is definitely on its way. I do not believe that we shall have true democracy in this country until the second of these two groups has been placed in power. However, until that time arrives I think it is necessary that members on all sides of the house do everything in their power to get the government to remove some of the most grievous injustices which exist throughout the country at the present time in order to impress upon the people that they are sincere when they talk of a new social order. Furthermore, I think it is up to us to do our best to prevent them from taking steps that will endanger the success of the future peace.
I would say that the success of the future peace is bound to depend upon our ability to make it possible for all nations to give their people the greatest possible degree of economic and social security. The Atlantic charter is supposed to provide for that type of security. I would say that our ability to achieve that objective will depend to a large extent upon the degree to which we are prepared to' adopt the principle laid down by the Prime Minister when speaking before the Canadian federation of labour. At that time he stated that the only limit to our productive capacity was our resources and our will and skill to use them. I have pointed out already that this principle is not new, that it was recognized back in the period 1914 to 1919. It is apparently recognized to-day; yet it was denied during the peace from 1919 to 1939. I am afraid there is every indication that it will be denied again at the conclusion of this war. There are many indications pointing to that very thing.
An important point to notice in that regard is that the statement made by the Prime Minister is only true just as long as there is a nationally managed currency. It would not be true if you were on a gold basis; it would not be true if you were on a gold standard or if you tied your currency to an international currency based upon gold. You are then introducing another restriction which has absolutely nothing to do with the productive capacity of the country.
Take the situation that developed in this country at the start of the war. At that time we were on a 25 per cent gold basis. It was recognized that if we were to have a total war effort it would be necessary to increase our production to its full capacity. Both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance said that no financial restrictions would be allowed to impede that war effort and therefore we were forced off the gold basis. There 72537-28
is not one dollar of gold behind our money to-day. Surely it must be evident that if it is impossible, on a gold basis, to maintain our
production at its maximum capacity in order to put forward a maximum war effort, it will also be impossible to have a maximum peace effort if we are on a gold basis. We would be introducing artificial restrictions.
I do not wish to labour this point unduly. I am emphasizing it because there is every indication that a number of the united nations are intending to become a party to an international currency based upon gold. Among these nations we find the United States of America, Great Britain and apparently Canada. A year ago the Prime Minister denied this fact when I brought this question up in the house. I wonder if he is prepared to deny that fact to-day? I doubt it. This afternoon, when replying to a motion of mine for the production of certain papers, he stated that no commitments had been made, but he was not sure whether or not there had been any correspondence and he would have to get the permission of the United States and Great Britain before he could table that correspondence. Last year he said there had been no correspondence; this year he did not know whether there had been any. In so far as commitments are concerned, it must be remembered that one can say that there have been no commitments right up to the time the signature is placed on the paper. The commitments may be practically in existence to-day although nothing has actually been signed. Again I say that there is every indication that Canada has agreed to become a party to an international currency based upon gold. First of all I should like to refer to a statement which I read in the house last year in connection with the Rio conference. This was reported in the Edmonton Journal of January 21, 1940, and it reads as follows:
Creation of a free international exchange currency to facilitate flow of goods and prevent delay in transactions. It would be on a gold basis and in addition to the American nations, Great Britain, China, the Netherlands, India and all British dominions would enter into the agreement. A pool of allied gold holdings would be created. The Latin American countries would agree to peg their national currencies into the ' free international exchange currency.
I asked the Prime Minister whether or not Canada had any commitments, and he said that Canada had not any commitments and that there had not been any correspondence on this matter. It seems strange that it should be stated at the Rio conference that Canada had become a party or had agreed to such a proposal. At the same time I referred also to

The Address-Mr. Quelch

a speech made by the chairman of the seven-man post-war reconstruction committee, Doctor Cyril James. A speech which he made in Philadelphia is reported in the Toronto Daily Star of September 17, 1940, as follows:
He declared that the United States gold holdings now exceeding $21,000,000,000 were at stake in the war and that their value would depend on who won. A British victory meant continuance of gold as the monetary medium whereas a German victory, as Doctor Funk himself recently made bluntly clear, would mean the setting up of regional autarchies in which gold would be useless except for economic decoration. Another definite reason, if any were required, for Canadians doing their utmost, in war loans and everything else, for the defeat of Germany! One of our greatest industries is gold mining and, to protect our economic order as well as our country and our homes, victory must be assured.
In commenting on that I pointed out that it was quite evident that Doctor Cyril James had a definite opinion that Canada was prepared to return to the gold standard after the war. The Minister of Pensions was in the house at that time and emphatically denied that there was any danger of that occurring. I wonder if the minister would still be prepared to deny to-day that Canada was playing any part in the introduction of an international currency based on gold.
I have two more quotations of recent date which clearly indicate that Canada is at present very much interested in this matter. I quote first from Trend, a Canadian News Letter, published at 231 St. James street west, Montreal. On the back page of its issue of February 5, 1943, under the heading "international currency" I read this:
1.	Great Britain and the United States are agreed on the necessity for continued and rigid control of international currency fluctuations.
2.	Plans are being made for creation of currency control machinery which will include extension of the "stabilization fund" idea and the redistribution of America's vast hoard of gold.
3.	The currency rates of all countries will be tied together, and governed by the rate fixed for the British pound and the American dollar.
4.	Leading nations will ascertain that such rates be maintained, regardless of adverse developments.
5.	A new monetary unit-a "world dollar"- will be introduced for the stabilization of all moneys.
Canada will participate in this scheme of monetary rearrangement.
There does not seem to be any uncertainty with regard to that statement.
To come back to the government, another statement was made over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's network last year on behalf of the government that the Prime Minister wished to assure the people that just

because "we were curtailing the production of gold it did not mean that the government had lost confidence in gold." What does confidence in gold mean if it does not mean confidence in the gold standard? When you say that you have confidence in gold it means that you believe in gold as a monetary unit. Quite evidently the Prime Minister did not appreciate what his own statement meant when he said that the only limit upon our productive capacity was our resources and our skill and will to use them and at the same time says that he has confidence in gold. You cannot use your productive capacity to the limit when at the same time you believe in that automatic limitation which would exist under the gold standard. I did not think it possible that there could be in the government to-day people who would be prepared to say they still believe in the gold standard. I recall the statement made by Lord Sempill in the House of Lords in November, 1941, that no progressive people anywhere believed in the gold standard, that the only people who believed in it-he should have paged1 the Prime Minister-were museum pieces and gold-bugs. Unfortunately in the past we have had too many elderly ostriches on the treasury benches who have dug their heads so deeply into the sands of reaction that they are unable to face the realities of life.
Here is a statement that merits serious consideration. It was referred to in the Montreal Star of February 2. It is the statement made by Sir Kingsley Wood, Chancellor of the British Exchequer. I quote:
Turning to the future of world trade, the chancellor said:
"We want to secure an economic policy agreed between the nations and an international monetary system which will be the instrument of that policy.
"This means that if any government is tempted to move too far either in inflationary or deflationary directions it would be subject to check."
Mark well the significance of that statement. An international authority is to have the power to check any programme of expansion in any country if it considered that expansionary movement as being inflationary. The international authority apparently would be the sole judge as to whether or not a country's programme was inflationary. Just imagine for one minute what would happen if on that international authority there were men of the type and mentality of the former Minister of Finance of this government, the Hon. Charles Dunning! I recall that time and again in this house during the period from 1935 to 1939, when he was pressed to start on a programme of monetary expansion so as to put unemployed to work in order to build up the

The Address-Mr. d'Anjou
wealth of the country, he made the never to be forgotten reply that it would be crude inflation. That is what he always called it whenever we suggested that the unemployed be put to work on developing the resources of this country to provide a higher standard of living. I remember that at one time the actual sum of $200,000,000 was mentioned, and the Hon. Mr. Dunning became perfectly hysterical at the thought of putting $200,000,000 into circulation to put the unemployed to work. Yet to-day we are bringing down budgets of five and six billion dollars! But remember the Hon. Charles Dunning was held in very high esteem by financial institutions in this country from one end to the other, right through that period from 1935 to 1939. Presidents of banks, loan corporations and other financial institutions all praised the wonderful mentality and financial capacity of the Hon. Charles Dunning. That is undoubtedly the type of man you would have on your international authority, with power to prevent any nation from bringing into force a programme of expansion. It would be prevented on the ground that it was inflationary.
This is supposed to be a war, Mr. Speaker, between the democracies and dictatorships, but if this proposal is put into force we shall have an international financial dictatorship. We shall win the war but lose the peace, and in that event, in the words of the Right Hon. David Lloyd George we would be guilty of the basest perfidy that ever blackened a people's fame, and our sons' sons in less than twenty years from now might very well become engaged in another war, a civil war if not an international war. I have emphasized this fact because when we recall the tremendous sacrifices that were made in the last war and appreciate the tremendous sacrifices that are being made again to-day, we cannot afford to make the same mistake as we made after the last war. Some people will say: That is a matter for the experts to decide. Our troubles of the past have been brought about by these so-called financial experts, and I think it is high time that the people of the country use a little common sense themselves in dealing with the situation in order to make sure that an international financial dictatorship will not be imposed upon this country and other peoples of the world.
My time is rapidly passing. Before concluding, I should like to make a few comments on the amendments. We will support the main amendment; we will also support the amendment to the amendment which has been moved by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I might point out that their amendment is very similar to a number of amendments which 72537-28}
this group has moved in the house from time to time since the declaration of war. We have emphasized in the past that we believe in a pay-as-you-go policy. We should realize that the real cost of the war is being met to-day. We therefore believe that the financial cost should be met at the same time. Such a policy, a pay-as-you-go policy, would not reduce the standard of living of the people in the slightest degree. There is so much production available that production can still be made available to the people no matter what the government's financial policy may be. But the great difference between a pay-as-you-go policy and the present type of policy would be that by the end of the war we would not have increased our debt, instead of allowing, as we are allowing to-day, a small percentage of the people to accumulate claims, in the form of bonds, against a very large percentage of the future production of wealth. We contend that this is unfair, because our soldiers are now making the greatest sacrifice they should be called upon to make. When they go overseas they are making what should be considered the supreme sacrifice. Yet, as a result of the policy we have in operation to-day, when our soldiers, our sailors and our airmen come back they will be called upon to help pay the financial cost. We consider there can be no possible justification for that situation.
Mr. J. E. S. EMMANUEL d'ANJOU (Rimouski) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, my reason for speaking at this time, is that I wish to make my stand absolutely clear both before this house and before the whole country'.
On March 26, 1940, the electors of the beautiful constituency of Rimouski conferred on me the great honour of returning me to parliament as their representative. Consequently, I cannot let this occasion pass without assuring them of my enduring gratitude.
I must sincerely say that my reelection by my constituents is due, in a great measure, to the fact that I have always been opposed to conscription. I was opposed to it in 1917, in 1940, and I am still more opposed to it in 1943.
My feelings and my attitude on the ticklish question of conscription have not changed; I remain an unshakable opponent of compulsory military service for overseas and no .power on earth could incite me to alter by a single iota my firm stand on this knotty problem.
During the 1940 election campaign I ran as the official candidate of the King-Lapointe government, opposing conscription for service overseas.
The Address-Mr. d'Anjou

I accepted the official Liberal candidature because I had full confidence in the leaders of the government who were then promising that compulsory military service for overseas would never be enacted in Canada by an administration under their leadership and as long as they would preside over the destinies of the country.
With every reason to believe in the sincerity and frankness of the Liberal leaders, I took the solemn pledge of voting, in this house, against any government who would attempt to enforce conscription for overseas service. I added that I would not hesitate a single moment to vote against my own party if it ever decided to enact compulsory military service for any place outside the Canadian territory. I took this solemn pledge to all my constituents and, God helping, I have kept it and intend to remain faithful to it in the future.
However, the leaders of the Liberal party, forgetful of their formal undertaking toward the electors of the whole country, altered their views and had the majority of the members of this house vote for the hideous conscription measure for overseas service.
First, the government submitted to the approval of parliament a bill authorizing them to hold a plebiscite to know w'hether they should be relieved of the anticonscriptionist pledges they had taken during the 1940 electoral campaign.
Realizing as I did that such a measure, if passed, would inevitably lead to conscription, I opposed it with the utmost energy and I voted against it with great readiness. The bill was passed by a very strong majority and the government took advantage of that fact to order the holding of a plebiscite on April 27 last. As a result of a carefully planned campaign, which took place over the radio and in the press, the government had an overwhelming majority of "Yes" votes in eight of the Canadian provinces, but the province of Quebec gave a huge majority of "No" votes, and I am proud to say that 94 per cent of the voters in my constituency replied in the negative.
What is more, Mr. Speaker, over 700,000 negative votes were registered in the rest of the country.
However, the government gave no heed to that warning, and such a landslide of negative votes did not impress them.	[DOT]
Therefore, a fortnight after the plebiscite, they requested the house to amend section 3 of the 1940 Mobilization Act, so as to extend compulsory military service for overseas.

After a protracted and acrimonious debate, the heinous conscription for service outside Canadian borders was passed by a majority of the members of this house. In keeping with the firm stand I had taken on the plebiscite bill, I voted against the government's amendment enacting compulsory military sendee for overseas. What the Hon. Mr. Godbout, premier of the province of Quebec, had called a " national crime " became an accomplished fact and the crime was consummated. I for one have the satisfaction of having done my duty, all my duty toward those I have the honour and the privilege of representing in this parliament. And to be consistent, I reserve the right to he at variance with and vote against the government whenever they introduce measures or bills conflicting with the principles for the defence of which I was elected and which I will continue to defend in this house.
Mr. Speaker, that is my position, my stand before this parliament and before the leaders of the present government.
Mr. Speaker, I should like for a few moments to deal with the agricultural question, which is of particular interest to me. Agriculture offers to-day our most alarming problem and as representative of an agricultural constituency, whose whole population has remained firmly rooted to the land, I feel it my duty to rise in this debate and defend its rights.
I personally believe that this government has been too tardy in doing its duty to the farmers of this country. Since the outbreak of hostilities, I have been of the opinion that the government did not take the agricultural situation seriously. But now that our military training camps are filled with farmers' sons they seem to realize its seriousness.
In Rimouski county, there are at least 1,400 young men in one military camp. Of these, two thirds are farmers' sons, notwithstanding the fact that during the last session assurance was given by the government that farmers' sons and farm workers would be exempted. That w'as merely a bluff. The farmers and their sons have been subjected to so many difficulties when claiming exemptions that very few, if any, have succeeded in getting them.
Nevertheless, farmers are being asked to increase their production, to produce more and more. I heard the other day a public speaker, an official of the Dominion Department of Agriculture, asking farmers to increase their production of pork and of all kinds of

The Address-Mr. d'Anjou
live stock. He invited farmers to grow more potatoes and to increase their production by all possible means.
But how are farmers to increase their production when they are deprived of the needed help? The difference between agriculture and the war industries is that the first produces life while the latter produce death. Farmers feed not only the civilian population, but also the soldiers who are called to the colours. If our soldiers are to fulfil their duties efficiently, they must be fed and well fed. No matter how well they are equipped or armed, if they are given nothing to eat, what will be their value as soldiers in the defence of their country?
This session, the mistake made by the government since the outbreak of the war is claimed to have been realized and it is suggested that farmers and their sons be exempted from military service. A document signed by the director of the selective service and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) says that henceforth farmers now living on the farm are to be exempted from military service. Is that merely a repetition of what happened last year, is that more bluff? I hope not.
However, if the government are sincere, if they really wish farmers and their sons to remain on the farm, I ask them to go somewhat further and to recall from training camps all the farmers and farmers' sons who are actually under training and to return them to their farms. This the government would do if they really wished to help agriculture which, everything considered, is the mainstay of the nation. The land is the great feeder and if the government really and sincerely wish to show a practical interest in agricultural matters, their first important measure should be, I repeat it, to return all enlisted farmers to their farms. In training camp No. 55, at Rimouski, two-thirds of the trainees are farmers' sons and I ask the government to return these young men to the farm instead of forcing them to pursue their military training.
A few days ago, certain individuals appeared in the constituency of Rimouski. In a hotel in Rimouski, there are, at present, 60 provosts-you may call them by whatever name you please-or military police hunting the defaulters and the deserters, those who failed to report for military service and those who deserted the training camp. I do not condone this policy. I remember too well what happened in 1917 and 1918. We then severely criticized the Union government, because they hunted farmers' sons even in the most remote
forests of the counties and then incarcerated them in the common gaols of the county seats.
I remember seeing 400 young farmers crowded in the Rimouski gaol for failing to report. I wish to ask why the government is acting in this way. Why are they sending these provosts or military police to terrorize our population by hunting farmers' sons who have failed to answer the call for military service in a training camp? What was wrong in 1917 and 1918 is not commendable in 1943, under a Liberal administration. Personally, I condemn this system.
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the speech delivered by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) the other day. He took pride in being able to state before parliament and the people that of all the allied nations, Canada, with a population of eleven million and a half inhabitants, was the one which had made the greatest contribution to the war effort. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that is a matter for pride. Canada to-day has under arms 700,000 men. She has supplied to her allies not only food but war weapons. Finally, as was said by the Prime Minister, she has made a greater contribution than any other country. Well, this is a proper time for thinking more than ever before, and I wish to say for the second time that we have a good opportunity not only to tell our farmers and their sons to remain on their farms, but to authorize those who are now in training to return home, to go back to the farm. In so doing the government will realize that agriculture is of prime importance and that, more than ever, Canadian farmers must have some consideration from the government and the people's representatives.
Now, Mr. Speaker, even though we are at war, the situation can be faced from a practical standpoint. Mine is not the only constituency where there are rural mail carriers. That is true of most constituencies. I understand that those mail carriers obtain tlieir contracts by tender. That is no reason for paying them an insufficient salary. That is no reason for starving them. Most of these people, especially in these times, and in the winter season, labour under great difficulties, and for them as for the whole population, the cost of living has increased. Therefore, I make a special appeal to the Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock) asking him to consider the case of our rural mail carriers, whose services are extremely valuable to the public, and I am convinced that the Postmaster General will try to improve their condition. The mail service is also inadequate because in some remote sections of Rimouski, mail deliveries
The Address-Mr. d'Anjou

are made only once or twice a week. That is not adequate. I have often asked for more frequent deliveries, but was told: "This is war. Let us win it first, and we will then deal with that matter." Well, Mr. Speaker, after the war the world will not come to an end, and in the meantime those people must live.
When a billion dollar gift is made to England and a further gift is being considered, I fail to see any good reason for the post office department not granting the legitimate claims of these rural mail carriers in my constituency.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate my friend the energetic member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) for having brought to the attention of the house to-day a question in which I am deeply interested. He spoke of the newly created national war labour board. Even since I became a member I have noticed how in Ottawa French Canadians were being flouted, how no opportunity to ignore their rights is overlooked and in the present instance, I believe the government has been ill-advised in setting up a new national war labour board without appointing a single French Canadian on it. It seems that for one member out of three, namely one-third of the representation on that board, to have been a French Canadian would not have been exaggerated. I was hoping that the government would show more fairness to my compatriots. In this instance, I regret to find that the government has overlooked the fact that English and French Canadians enjoy equal rights in this country guaranteed by the pact of confederation. It is never too late to mend one's ways and I hope the government will appoint a French Canadian to represent us on that national war labour board.
I have made these remarks, Mr. Speaker, with the utmost frankness and I believe I can state as I resume my seat that I have fulfilled my task and -I feel satisfied that I have done my duty.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne falls naturally into two main divisions: first, our progress in the world war and, second, the social problems at home. In both these spheres there are certain aspects which will bear watching very carefully by every Canadian. We remember what happened in 1918, and how it formed the basis for the catastrophe that we are facing in the world to-day. In just the same way what we do in 1943 may easily form the basis for another catastrophe in a few years, with an interlude which will be nothing but a period of rationed poverty, unemployment, want and fear. We must take

steps now to prevent that. Frankly, we can see very little hope either for the prevention of the world war of 1960, or for the solving of our other problems under the old administrations, for the simple reason that neither of the old parties will recognize the fact that basic and radical changes must come about in the economic order.
On the war front magnificent retreats and disgraceful surrenders have been fewer on the western and southern fronts. On the Russian front conditions are much more hopeful. The lifting of the siege of Stalingrad, the recapture of Rostov, the recent brilliant successes of- the Russian winter offensive, are sources of the greatest satisfaction to us and the greatest hope for the allied cause. When the history of this world war is properly written I think it will be said that democracy was saved in 1942 at the gates of Stalingrad. In contrast, however, we had the disgraceful rise of Darlan to power in Africa. Fortunately his rise was cut short, but such things give the world cause for serious thought. There is evidence that there are Quislings in the allied nations; that the Chamberlains have heirs and successors; that the Cliveden set and the Oswald Mosleys are still at large. We have had allied conferences at which China and Russia were not represented.
Canadians are making sacrifices on many fronts. Canadians deserve the right of proper representation in order to bring forward the Canadian point of view at the peace conference; and at that conference these allies to whom I have referred, Russia and China, must sit round the table and have something to say in the establishment of peace and the reconstruction of the world. We must face the possibility that the Atlantic charter may easily become as empty a gesture as the fourteen points of President Wilson in 1918. There are three basic things of which Canadians must make sure at this time: first, that this war will not end until fascism and nazism are completely destroyed; second, that those internationally responsible for this war are brought to justice and prevented from carrying on their plans; third, that the foundations are laid for economic democracy throughout the world as one means of preventing a recurrence of this catastrophe and one step toward giving the rights of the common man to all people. Already there is evidence that there are too many people, even within this country of ours, who fear real social change just as much as they fear Hitler.
The' second phase of the speech from the throne deals with the problems of social security here at home, in these words:

The Address-Mr. Castleden
In Canada, a considerable measure of social security has already been provided through federal enactments establishing annuities, unemployment insurance and pensions for the aged, the blind and for disabled veterans; and through provincial enactments related to accidents, sickness and hospitalization, widows' and mothers' allowances and maternity benefits. There is, however, no approach to a nation-wide plan of social security.
Apparently the government imagines that already we have some large measure of social security. Words like those in the speech from the throne are not sufficient. We must look to the acts of the government for proof of its sincerity; and it is not to be wondered at that the people of Canada are sceptical when they hear phrases such as these used by governments which have administered this country since its inception, and under which this wealthy land has been brought to a condition of debt and destitution. In no land on the globe have the opportunities for good living been more abundant, but nowhere has the failure to provide a good living been so complete. Canadians as a whole consider that they have been completely duped by the old, wealthy and powerfully backed political parties of Canada. Since confederation the administrators of Canada have done two things effectively. In the first place they have handed over the resources of this dominion to privileged groups, and in the second place they have fortified these groups in their position by establishing laws to protect their powers to continue their exploitation.
Such administrations cannot institute real social reform. What is their record? To-day the farmer in Canada finds himself hopelessly in debt. Ilis insecurity is complete; there is fear on every side. No matter how he toils, there is no assurance that his toil will provide him with anything like a decent standard of living. Now in war time he finds that the prices bf many of his commodities are frozen at levels which are below the cost of production. He is constantly urged by this administration to continue the production of his goods; he is encouraged to go into mixed farmihg and to grow more coarse grains.
On March 24 last he was assured by no less a person than the Prime Minister that his labour would be kept on the farm. These are the words of the Prime Minister, as reported on page 1567 of Hansard in dealing with the farm labour problem;
On the other hand, the growing scarcity of labour on the farms and the increasing importance of maintaining, and indeed of increasing food production, has been recognized. This has been accomplished by a fundamental alteration of the policy regarding compulsory military training and service where such service touches persons wholly or mainly employed in agriculture. Up to the present there has been a general obligation to serve, and the responsibility for proving a case for postponement of service has rested with the individual. Under the new regulations, farmers, farmers' sons and agricultural labourers will normally not be obliged to undertake compulsory military training and service. It is realized, however, that in a limited number of cases, men on the farms are not, in fact, essential agricultural workers. If it is established to the satisfaction of the national war services boards concerned that such persons are not essential workers in agriculture, they will continue to be called for service in the appropriate age groups.
What do we find? I should like to read a letter I received the other day which illustrates the fact very well. It reads:
My son Peter-got his call and pass on the 26th of January stating that on 1st February he was supposed to be in Regina. He just sent it back asking for a postponement. Then on February 5 this call or pass came back saying he was to be in Regina on February 8. So went on the 8th.
There is something I would like to know why is it so that Peter my only son I have, and he has no father, just him to work half section of land and do everything still support me and my daughter; and other families around here with three or four boys in one family to work and yet that have a dad able to work. They got their calls before my son and they are still home. Some sent calls back like my son for about two months and had no answer. Some asked for postponement and got it. Why my son had only a week's time between the sending of the call back and receiving it. It sure is hard to understand.
My husband died and I was left alone with young children my son being only nine years. He supported me and my daughter from the age of sixteen years.

On the other hand, the president of the maritime federation of agriculture declared recently, upon his return from Ottawa where he attended joint meetings of federal and provincial agricultural officials, that a conflict of ideas among the heads of those agencies entrusted with the administration of the many phases of food production and distribution was largely responsible for the present state of confusion. This confusion, Mr. Oulton added, was causing additional trouble for the farmer rather than helping in the solution of his problems.
Instead of having a definite, clear-cut policy which would assure each agricultural unit which maintains a certain production that it would be guaranteed some labour on that farm and that labour would be left to it, what do we find? The farmer is left in uncertainty and insecurity. There is no definite policy at all; it is entirely up to these boards. The Prime Minister promises one thing and the boards
The Address-Mr. Castleden

do something entirely different. Cases similar to that which I have cited can be repeated by the dozen. When a farmer does not know how long his labour will be left to him, when his labour will be called up, how can he possibly plan mixed farming or the raising of cattle? Constant insecurity; constant uncertainty I The farmer has to put in all his applications for bonus. After being assured that the government wants all the coarse grain he can grow, he gets busy and grows one of the greatest crops ever produced. But now he finds that he cannot deliver it. He also finds that his wheat crop cannot be delivered. On the day the house opened the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) informed the Canadian people that the wheat delivery quotas in many parts of the country were now up to fourteen bushels an acre, but he did not tell us how many hundred thousands of farmers living in those areas where that quota is established cannot deliver that crop because there is no room in the elevator.
Most Canadian farmers are in debt. That is a problem which will have to be solved before we provide social security for the people of Canada. In many instances one-third of the crop must be delivered in the elevator in the name of the creditor. The farmer produces his crop. He puts it in the granary if he has one. He has done everything he can to pay off his debt. He tries to deliver it but is not allowed to. Surely he has paid his part of the bargain. But he still has to pay the interest on the money he owes until the law permits him to deliver his grain. You see how well the laws are set up always to protect capital. Sometimes, in cases that I have had brought to my attention, he is threatened with foreclosure by the mortgage company for not delivering the creditor's one-third of the crop. But he is not allowed to deliver it; there is no room in the elevator. He has done everything in his power, but he is tied hand and foot.
What is the position of labour? Wages are frozen at levels which represent an income of less than $1,000 a year for eighty-five per cent of the wage-earners in Canada. In Ontario they were frozen as low as fourteen cents an hour in some instances. Basic rates of wages in some of the essential industries in Quebec are from twenty-four cents to thirty-five cents an hour. What has the worker to look forward to? When the war is over, the bonus will be taken off in the interest of the employ-' ing class of Canada. That is why there is unrest in Canada. Labour in many instances works seven days a week, with no holidays, no security for the future. Therefore there is
IMr. Castleden.]
unrest and absenteeism. This government pays lip-service to the right of the workers to organize, but at the same time every stop-block that can be invented is placed in their way to prevent them from organizing. The industrial workers of Canada are filled with confusion; they are frustrated. That is not the spirit which will produce the goods and things needed in this war. The government should bring down legislation making recognition of organized labour and the right of collective bargaining compulsory on every employer in Canada. That is what is done in Great Britain.
Then take the matter of old age pensions. The young and the old, the blind and the crippled, and those who cannot take care of themselves should be the first care of every nation that calls itself civilized and that hopes to have the people look to an administration for social security such as we are told about in the speech from the throne. The most glaring example of the social attitude of the administrations of Canada in the past has been the neglect of these people who are unable to provide for themselves. I should like to read from a letter from one of these men; it will state the matter more plainly than I can myself. It reads:
Dear Sir,-
I am writing to you to complain of the attitude of the dependents' allowance board. We raised our grandson from childhood and who is now in the R.C.A.F.
We have applied for dependents' allowance and as we are both old age pensioners we are informed that they cannot do anything for us.
If this is all they can do after we have given up for the service the boy who helped to support us in our old age, then there is nothing for us to do but lay down as we are not getting the nutrition that we need. This is how we are placed. Out of our joint pension of $40 per month we have $20 rent monthly, light and heat to provide for, so you will readily see what we have left for food, etc.
It means that unless something is done for us that our home will have to be broken up and our hopes of eventide disappear.
Our only son (married) is overseas with the R.H.L.I. and now the grandson is with the R.C.A.F. Our all given to freedom's cause. Myself veteran of world war No. 1.
It is not gratitude or anything else on the part of the allowance board that is shown us. We are only asking for what we consider the right thing for our sacrifices.
What can people expect in the way of social reform when this happens?
Take the field of education, for instance. The failure to establish minimum standards of education and compulsory education throughout Canada for children up to the age of sixteen years is a thing which cannot be

The Address-Mr. Castleden
endorsed by thinking Canadians. The federal government should undertake to see to it that every Canadian is provided with an opportunity to obtain education; that it be made compulsory for children to attend school at least until the age of fifteen years. Furthermore, this government should see to it that the young people of our nation are given an education enabling them to do their part in service toward their fellowmen. Government subsidies and bursaries should be available for our young men and women who show ability in the schools. Some day a government will sit in those benches, a government that realizes that the brains of the young people of a country are the finest national resource and asset of any nation. Some day the training of those young people will not be dependent upon the wealth or-poverty of their parents, upon whether rain happened to fall on a farm for two or three years.

How many young men or young women in Canada leaving our public or high schools have had an opportunity to continue their education in a higher field? In the field of social service, Canada's care of its war veterans of the last war and the policies of the soldier settlement board are a blot on the administrations of this country.
There is evidence already that the veterans of this war, even under the highly lauded scheme of the present administration, are suffering hardship and neglect which should not exist. I came across this case in my own constituency. A young man still in uniform happened to be at one of my meetings. I asked him what he was doing now and he told me he had been discharged. I asked him why and he said he had been a motorcyclist overseas, but that during manoeuvres he had been side-swiped by a truck and had suffered a severe fracture of the bone above the left knee. He said that he had been sent to hospital, but that unfortunately cancer of the bone had set in and he had been returned home. He had been undergoing treatment, and when I asked him what pension he was receiving he said none at all. I asked if he had received a clothing allowance and he said he had. I quote from his letter:
I have received 28 or more treatments and have not received any since, only that I had to report back at the hospital in Regina every month since. Received the treatment in Regina Grey Nuns hospital. They quit giving me treatments on October 16.
I have spent on travelling, November 16, $8.10 and on December 18, $8.10, and now again
on February 18 will cost me another $8.10, which will amount to $24.30 on travelling alone and expenses besides cost me $7.50.
In another letter, he says:
Why should they cut my pay off and not start my pension as I was in to see them once about it and wrote twice and no answer or anything? What would be your opinion? Also they took my overcoat and overshoes away.
When I drew this matter to the attention of the board here I must say that they took immediate action. They arranged for an immediate investigation' of the case and placed the man on temporary one hundred per cent allowance, and the authorities were notified. Any government with such a long record of failure in the social field does not deserve nor will it retain the confidence of the people.
For those who are so smugly satisfied with what our governments have done in the past, I should like to read an extract from a pamphlet entitled, "Health on the March" which was issued by the Canadian federation of agriculture. In dealing with what has been done in New Zealand it said:
The results of New Zealand's plan for social security are already showing a great increase in the birth rate. For instance, when the labour government came into office, the birth rate was at its lowest level, 16-17 per 1,000 of population. In 1937, it rose to 16-64; 1937 saw a further rise to 17-29; 1938 to 17-93; 1939 to 18-73. After the maternity benefit was introduced in 1940, it rose to 2i-19; and 1941 to 22-81.
The story told by these figures is a tribute to the labour government, in a period in which the birth rate is still declining in most countries of the world. There has also been a decline of absenteeism in industry, due to illness; and an increased rate of production.
This is a lesson to us. Here we are, with the heritage of one half of a continent, and a totally inadequate population to develop it. You would think that we would have come to our senses long ago, and developed our human resources to the utmost.
Referring to the soviet union, the writer states:
From a condition of revolution, famine and disease; utter poverty; with 90 per cent of their people unable to read or write, they sprang from the age of candle-light, skipped the gas-light age, and emerged into the electrical age in a few years. What has been accomplished since 1922 is almost unbelievable to us, who are accustomed to the slow process of evolution of capitalist states.
And again:
It seems to me that the following four points represent the most characteristic features of the soviet health system. 1. Medical service is free and therefore available to all. 2. The prevention of disease is in the foreground of all health activities. 3. All health activities are directed by central bodies, the people's commissariats of health, with the result that 4. Health can be planned on a large scale.
The Address-Mr. Castleden

There can be no doubt that the soviet system of social insurance is infinitely superior to any insurance system in capitalist countries. The costs are what they should be, part of the cost of production. The benefits are infinitely greater than under any other insurance scheme. The worker is guaranteed complete medical service, he is given social security. He is entitled to it because, after all, he is creating the values that make such a scheme possible.

A former minister of health of the Alberta government, I believe. That is the soviet union, the country that is doing so much to save democracy to-day, the country that is showing such surprising reserves. The Canadian people, learning this, will not go back to the old regime of unemployment and want. The men who return from this war where they have risked everything to save and extend the democratic way of life will not be frustrated in their efforts to obtain a decent livelihood. There will be no constitutional difficulties placed in their way, difficulties laid down by the dead hand of the past in such things as the British North America Act. The laws of the land made to protect financial and industrial exploiters must be changed in a democratic way to suit the new order.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) seems to have started a sort of blitzkrieg in the house when he proposed representation in the House of Commons for the armed forces and recommended that the elections act should be amended to that end. I endorse what he said in that regard. The war of 1914-1918 was won on the battlefield, but the peace was lost to the politicians and the international bankers. I believe that the armed forces should have representation in the House of Commons. They should be permitted to nominate their candidates freely and to have free discussion of the issues within their own units. That was denied to them before, although they had the right to vote in the election of 1940. Their representation in the house should be in the same ratio of population that determines the election of members in the various constituencies throughout Canada. In this way we shall get the opinions, hopes and aspirations of the rank and file of the men and women of the armed forces who are doing their bit so nobly to-day. We want their voice heard in the reorganization of the world.
The old economic order is utterly incapable of giving security or freedom from want and fear. Economic democracy must be established. By that we mean that the resources
I Mr. Castleden.]
and the machinery of production of the nation must be democratically owned by the people and operated for the people. Then each person will be given his share of the nation's wealth in cultural advantages and economic security to satisfy his needs, and that in turn will be the incentive which will draw from each according to his ability to give. The economic and social well-being of the people will be the first duty of the state. Then and then only will there be an end to fear and an end to need. Then we shall have a state where fear cannot exist, and where health, education and recreation will be a national achievement. Then the old and the young, the crippled and the blind, shall live without fear, and those who work, being the creators of all wealth, shall have a claim on that wealth to satisfy their human needs before capital be permitted to take its toll. Such a programme determined by Canadians in annual democratic conventions, democratically controlled by those who toil in Canada, is the aim and objective of this party. A democratically elected council in the province of Quebec recently discovered that the milk distribution in its area was ineffective and wasteful. They decided to set up a municipal milk distribution plan. The farmers who supplied the milk then got more for their product; the people who consumed the milk got the milk cheaper; the people with the lower incomes got more milk, and they are the ones who need it most. I suppose my hon. friends to my right would call that socialism. Well, if that is socialism, I am pleased to be called a socialist. To those who fear such a programme, who fear for the rights of property, I will give this assurance:	They will be permitted
to own anything except the right and the power to exploit their fellow men.
The amendment which has been moved by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation reads:
And further we regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to take the necessary action to achieve a total war effort by neglecting to apply the powers contained in the National Resources Mobilization Act to war industries and financial institutions in the same manner as they are being applied to the mobilization of man-power fey military service.
Those are the principles which we must follow in time of war if we are to fight a full and proper war, and when this war is won those are the principles which, being established in a democratic way, will make possible equality of opportunity in time of peace, just as there should be equality of sacrifice in time of war.

Mr. Speaker it is not my intention to run the whole gamut of the speech from the throne or to embark upon a review of world events. The speech from the throne has been discussed at great length, and it has been approved and condemned, eulogized and criticized. It has been called apt and inept, depending on the mood of the speaker and his political complexion. I intend to discuss but three paragraphs of the speech from the throne, and to discuss them briefly because there will be another opportunity to develop them at greater length.
At the very outset I should like to express my personal thanks and my own appreciation to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Mac-Nicol) for his continued interest in western Canada and in the province of Saskatchewan. The hon. gentleman has employed the time during the recess in visiting our western provinces in order to cultivate an all-Canadian viewpoint, and from personal experience he has found on the rolling prairies a home for countless millions in the future. And that hope is based upon what? He there finds the finest and largest continuous stretch of good agricultural land that lies out-of-doors anywhere. He has carried his explorations further. He has come to agree with us who reside on the prairies that ours is a badly balanced economy. In northern Saskatchewan, following those two great rivers, the North and South Saskatchewans, he has found potential power sites which will support industry to be established in the years to ctme. He agrees with the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Gregory), wdio described the gas fields that have been developed at Lloydminster, which could and should be used as a basis for industrial development; with the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Evans), also from our province, who knows all the deposits of pottery and building clays inexhaustible in their extent; with the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) in whose constituency are to be found huge deposits of china clays equal to the best to be found in the county of Kent, England; and with the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) who will take ten minutes off any time to elaborate upon the deposits of firebrick clay to be found in his constituency, and who will tell you, along with the hon. member for Davenport, that all the firebrick used in the fire boxes of the engines of the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National railways in the west are manufactured' south of Moose Jaw. If we go further south into the constituency of Assindboia, the hon. member (Mr. Tripp) rejoices with us that in, his constituency there are twenty
billion tons of lignite coal, with an overburden of from 40 to 150 feet. The value of that coal is emphasized in a little book I hold in my hand entitled "Brown Coal and Magic", It tells the story of how the brown coals of Australia have been developed and used to support cities of half a million-, and- their whole industrial development is based upon that coal. There is in the Estevan area a potential development of power in unlimited quantities. Not only that, but the coal we have in southern Saskatchewan is superior to that of Australia. Australian coal has a moisture content of 65 per cent, and ours has a moisture content of 30 per cent. Once again may I point out that the whole industrial development of Germany is based on the brown coals of that country. I need refer only to the dye industry and the chemical -industry. We have not even scratched the surface of this great potential natural resource.
Not only has -the hon. member for Davenport done us the honour to which I have referred, but he has done more, and I thank him for it most sincerely. He has come to eastern Canada and told the story to the sceptics, to the men and women who here, a few years ago, would have given the land back to the Indians. We invite him back to our province, and we shall be glad if he will continue his speeches in eastern Canada. I can assure him that he will have an evergrowing and ever more appreciative audience.
There is a passage in the speech from the throne to which I should like to make a brief reference. I do so because it is the subject-matter of many communications to myself, many editorials and news items in the newspapers and, I would say, it is uppermost in the minds of ninety-nine per cent of the taxpayers of this country. The passage is as follows:
These will include the further development of the method of payment of the personal income tax in the year in which income is received, thus carrying to its logical conclusion the approach made last year to the collection of taxes on a current basis.
In the popular mind and in the newspapers that plan is associated with the name of Beardsley Ruml, and in so far as the United States of America is concerned it is properly associated with 'him. But in- Canada that plan should be referred' to as the Hsley plan, for in the budget of last year the principle of that plan was introduced, and came into effect on the 1st day of September. For that reason I welcome the passage in the speech from the throne which indicates further progress of the pay-as-you-go policy in the matter of personal income. It will afford relief to a
The Address-Mr. McNiven

very large number of people who do not like to be ini debt to anyone, .even to their own government.
I should also like to make a brief reference to another matter referred to in the speech from the throne:
My ministers believe that a comprehensive national scheme of social insurance should be worked out at once which will constitute a charter of social security for the whole of Canada.
I will not enlarge upon that at any great length, for practically all of those who have preceded me have spoken on it and have agreed with the substance of that declaration in the speech from the throne. In that regard the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden), who preceded me, was no exception; but I must say that the nature of his remarks was decidedly different from the great majority of the contributions to this debate. I know the hon. member quite well; I also know the bon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) and the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas); I delight in having conversations with them, and I assure the house that in my personal conversations with these three hon. members they do not give birth to such statements as we hear from them on the floor of the house. Let me recall some of the remarks which have been made by the hon. member for Yorkton. He speaks of destitution, of Canadians being completely destitute. He speaks of lack of sincerity. He speaks of no assurance of living or of security. He speaks of frustration. He speaks of a blot against this country. He speaks about complaints. He speaks about a long record of failure. One would imagine, from what he has declared just within the last thirty minutes, that he and those associated with him had a monopoly on success, but I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that that is very far removed from the fact. Why, sir, he called upon this government to institute a minimum standard of education, and he criticized them severely 'because they had thus far failed to introduce a standardized1 system of education. Apparently he is not familiar with the British North America Act, which gives the provinces exclusive jurisdiction over education.
