speechtext:
When I read this resolution by hon. friend will wish that he had had a better lesson before he reached the Winnipeg convention. This is the resolution:
Whereas the present and future generations are greatly indebted to the pioneer for much of what we enjoy to-day;
And whereas the interests of Canada are best advanced by a healthy and robust citizenship;
And whereas the youth of Canada constitute its greatest asset;
And whereas the home is the foundation unit of every worth-while citizenship;
And whereas national strength is achieved proportionately as a nation assumes and per-
The Address-Mr. McNiven

forms its maximum duty to the aged, the pioneer, the unfortunate, the youth and the home:
Therefore be it resolved that the council of the Liberal association for the province of Saskatchewan unequivocally pledges the Liberal party of Saskatchewan to a policy of social security effective immediately, and the Liberal party will recommend to the Saskatchewan and dominion governments that such a policy of social security, without limiting the scope of such policy, shall include:
1.	An immediate increase of $5 in the monthly payment presently payable under the Old Age Pensions Act, and that a study of prevailing conditions applicable to the old age pensions be forthwith undertaken to determine the schedule of monthly payments which will provide an improved standard of living.
2.	An increase of the maximum annual income of the pensioner under the Old Age Pensions Act from $360 to $500.
3.	A progressive reduction in the age limit now fixed by the Old Age Pensions Act in order to provide openings in employment for the men and women now in the armed forces of Canada and likewise those engaged in war work.
4.	An adequate allowance to widows with small children and in particular those with large families to enable such widows to devote their time and attention to the care and upbringing of their children.
5.	An increase in the allowance presently made for each child under the mothers' allowance act.
6.	A substantial increase in the schedule of payments now made to sightless persons, together with improved facilities and greater opportunity for the training and advancement of those sightless persons who are below the age limit.
May I pause here to make this observation. It was this government that in 1927 introduced old age pensions. It was this government that, in 1937 or 1938, provided pensions for sightless persons. And now members have the temerity to charge this government with lack of sincerity and lack of consideration. It has not done all that we should like to have done, but surely it is not subject to that charge in any event. To continue:
7.	That a dominion-wide system of compulsory old age insurance be worked out and adopted at the earliest possible date with a variable age of retirement.
8.	That a dominion-wide system of compulsory contributory health insurance, or alternatively a dominion-wide contributory plan making provision for medical care and hospitalization be worked out and made effective at the earliest possible date.
9.	That the present scheme of unemployment insurance be carefully supervised in order to iron out existing inequalities and to extend its benefits to an ever-widening circle of employees.
And that for the purposes aforesaid the provincial and dominion governments assume by agreement their fair share of the financial responsibility involved, or alternatively that the government of Canada obtain the necessary authority by way of amendments to the British

North America Act to enable it to introduce legislation designed to give the widest possible security to the aged, the unfortunate, the youth, together with the largest possible measure of protection for the homes of Canada.
There stand the Liberal party of Saskatchewan, prepared to implement those parts of this scheme that lie within their jurisdiction. They have not carried it to the length they would wish, but they are looking confidently to the time when adequate provision will be made for those who are unable to take care of themselves and when the Liberal party of Saskatchewan will be in a position to implement that programme in its entirety.
With' regard to those who have criticized this government concerning old age pensions, I should like to hear from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) as to what, if any, representations have been made to him by the provinces since he declared in this house in November, 1941, that he would be willing to receive and consider any representations that might be made by all or a majority of the Canadian provinces for an increase in old age pensions. Not ' so long ago I saw in the press that the eastern provinces had not made any such representations though, if I know the Minister of Finance as I think I do, once having made that statement he will stand by it; and when the Canadian provinces, whose responsibility it is to care for aged persons, come to the dominion government they will be received by a gentleman who will listen to their plea. I am in favour of an increase in the old age pension. I have great respect for the pioneer, for the old man and the old woman, and I do not think we in this house, or the young men and young women of this country, should ever be allowed to forget the contribution that has been made to the development of this country by those old people. Much of what we enjoy to-day in our cities, our towns, our villages, our schools, in connection with our highways and so on, we owe to the enterprise, initiative, courage and financial contribution of many of those men and women who have since fallen upon evil days.
I was interested in reading a pamphlet issued by the much maligned public information department, called "Canada and the People's War," which I find replete with information. It gives an historical survey of the development of the armed forces and the industrial life of Canada, and after a perusal of this pamphlet there is no reason why every man and woman in this country should not be fully informed as to what Canada a>t war has accomplished. Canada has been at war for some forty-one months. A hurried review of the twenty years that preceded the declara-

The Address-Mr. McNiven
tion of war reveals that Canada had no foreign policy as this is known in other coun-' tries. Canada maintained1 no diplomatic service in the European capitals, nor was Canada concerned in any of the intrigues that went on there. Time and again during five years preceding the war the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stated that we have no commitments in Europe. Canada was not anxious to secure an improved position in the capitals of the world by arranging for the marriage of the Prime Minister, or the first leader of the present opposition, Viscount Bennett, or the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), into some of the royal families of Europe.
This country had no desire for territory which any other country possessed. Aggrandizement was not part of our policy, no matter what party was in power. Ours was a policy of being willing to trade, a policy which might be summarized as that of the open hand and the friendly gesture, a willingness to trade with anyone who would trade with us on a reasonably equal basis. For such a policy Canada needed no great armada, no immense standing army, no great aerial fleet, no great industry for the manufacture of munitions and warlike supplies. For these reasons Canada, in common with the other twenty-eight united nations including Great Britain and the United States, was caught totally unprepared for war. At that time the Prime Minister of Great Britain said that it would be three years before the democracies would be ready to meet the hun on his own terms. The Prime Minister of this country concurred in that statement, and made it a fundamental, primary principle of his policy that we should have unity at home as a pre-requisite to a maximum, balanced, continuous war effort from the beginning of the war until peace finally returned. That, sir, has been accomplished in splendid fashion, well within the time indicated by the hon. gentlemen. I distinctly recall during the last three years many people criticized this government for being slow, unwilling, wasteful; for lacking sincerity in the prosecution of the war. But to-day many of those critics are wondering in hushed tones if this government has not undertaken too much, if it has not embarked upon too great a programme for twelve million people. This afternoon we heard the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson), who was one of the severest critics of the government, give expression to a statement of that kind.
I started to say that this is a people's war. We find that in the three years of which Mr. Churchill spoke 721,000 of our young men and
women have rallied to the colours. We find that our output of munitions and the impedimenta of war has an annual value of about 3-7 billion dollars. We find that over a million people, of whom 145,000 are women, are employed in industry, and therefore we in this house, irrespective of our political affiliations, can join in paying tribute to the manner in which labour has worked with capital and capital has worked with labour in order to produce a continuous flow of munitions to the various war zones. Truly, sir, it is a people's war. Then, too, we come to the production of food on a threefold front-food for the civilians of this country, food for the armed forces of this country, and food for the nations, the allies of this country. Canadian farmers have responded1 to every call and 'have produced in unbelievable quantities, Which thanks to our fleet and our convoy system have been going across the Atlantic in an endless chain. I want to pay my tribute to our farmers for what they have accomplished and also to pay whole-hearted and sincere tribute to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for his guidance and planning and direction of that effort which has given such surprising and marvellous results.
Then in the matter of finance, there is scarcely a man or woman in this country who three years ago would have believed that Canada could bear and would submit to taxation in the huge amounts now required to meet our war expenditures. There are very few who would have even suggested that this country was capable of producing the immense sums of money which have been subscribed for the three victory loans. When we realize that Canada's vote for war purposes in the fiscal year 1942-43 with the supplementary estimates is approximately three times the entire amount spent by Canada in the whole of the last war we have some measure of the accomplishment of the Canadian people in financing this war. Truly, sir, it is a people's war, and the taxpayers of this country have responded nobly.
Every province is making its comparable contribution to this meritorious result, not even excepting the province of Saskatchewan, which has been so loudly berated this evening. Sometimes, because of the addresses delivered from time to time during the last six or seven years from the C.C.F. section of "the house our province has become known as the "orphan Annie", the poor relation, the unwanted child, of the Canadian family; some even go so far as to say, give it back to the Indians. But in those self same three years of which I speak, our province had recruited to the end of October 53,900 soldiers for the
The Address-Mr. McNiven

armed forces, and recruits have been pouring in since then at the rate of twelve hundred a month. I mentioned a moment ago that this is a people's war, irrespective of class, race or creed, and is so regarded in our province. There comes to my mind a citizen of the town of Wolseley, a French Canadian with seven sons, all of them in t'he armed forces, and Rudolph Deutcher, a German farmer at Odessa with eight sons, of whom six are in the armed forces, the seventh in an important war industry and the eighth impatiently waiting on the calendar until he can join his brothers. I think of a Jewish family at Kamsack with five sons in the armed forces; I think of old Mr. Reinlander in Regina, born in Russia, with four sons in the armed forces. My mind goes back to that sunny afternoon of August 8 with the Prime Minister present in our city when two women were presented to him-Mrs. Muirhead, of Estevan, of Scotch-Irish origin, and Mrs. Uren, of Regina, both she and her husband born in Austria. These two women were, presented to the Prime Minister and received from him his personal thanks and the thanks of the people of Canada because each of them had six sons and two sons-in-law in our armed forces.
I am using only a few illustrations, but I have no doubt every hon. member can multiply, times without number, illustrations such as I have used. I want to emphasize again that in our province and, I believe, in every province, this is a people's war, irrespective of class, race or creed.
This province of ours, sometimes known as the "orphan Annie" province, has been pictured as the special domain of the mortgage companies. What I protest against most vigorously is that the other side of the picture is never given by the C.C.F. section of the house. For their information and1 the information of hon. members generally I say that we in Saskatchewan are proud of our province, and I am going to put on the record some statistics in order to show what has been accomplished in the matter of production and -the increase in the last three years:

As to cattle, hon, members will remember the year 1937 when 375,000 head of our cattle were slaughtered because we had a complete crop failure on account of the drought. In 1939 Saskatchewan marketed 172,865 head of cattle, and in 1942 marketed 256,186. As to

hogs, listen to this: in 1939 we marketed 312,188; in 1942 we marketed 964,622. In the same period the annual marketing of sheep has increased from 63,807 to 88,908, and the production of creamery butter has increased from 25,000,000 pounds to over 41,000,000, pounds.
The farmers of Saskatchewan heard the call. Canada required butter, and they answered it by an increase in production of nearly 100 per cent. In 1935 our production of honey was a little over a million pounds. In 1942 it was approximately five million pounds. In lumber our production for 1939 was 37,974,000 feet, and last year it was 125,853,000 feet.
With regard to coal, of which I spoke a little while ago, the production in 1939 was 959,595 tons, and in 1942, 1299,891 tons, or an increase of 340,000 tons, and there are people all over western Canada who are grateful, on nights such as this, for that increased production.

If I fail this evening in extending the usual compliments to the mover and the seconder of the address, it is not on account of a lack of respect for those two hon. gentlemen, or for the uniform they wear; it is not because I have not a full appreciation of the contribution which they have made, but simply because so many previous speakers have paid compliments to them in a manner which I could not do. Therefore I shall let it go at that. Because of the time at my disposal I will change almost completely what I had intended to say. I should like to finish before eleven o'clock. I had hoped to use practically all my time on the speech from the throne itself, because I consider that this document will go down in history, either as one of great credit to this government or as one that will condemn it.
The other evening the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) said that it was a barren statement, but I do not agree with him. I think it has everything in it to make us proud. If we follow it out it will make for us a great nation, one of which we shall be proud, one worthy of the sacrifices of those who have gone before and of those who are fighting for us at the present time. But if we allow trivialities and politics to interfere with our path of progress, then we may easily expect confusion. I think we can say of this, to use the words of Robert Service:
The choice is ours, to make or mar
To count the ties, or drive a motor car.
If we choose to follow what is set out in the speech from the throne we can make out of it something worthwhile. But I shall not

The Address-Mr. Mayhew
say anything more about it at the present time because I want to deal with some other matters.
One thing about which I want to make my position clear is the pay of our junior officers in the army. The other night the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Ross) had something to say on this subject, with all of which I agreed. But there are some things he did not say which should be said. Most of the young men going into the armed services are leaving positions of importance. Many of them are professional men, and they are sacrificing much in the way of remuneration in
men upon whom we must depend for leadership; they are the type of men whom we would want our sons to follow when they are in the army. I certainly would; I would probably put them first. I am glad the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) is in his seat because I should like to refer to those soldiers who have been discharged from the army on account of tuberculosis. There are two men in the hospital at Victoria who went before the medical board, were attested and examined by the doctors, including X-ray examination of their chest; they went into the army and served for some months, I think for a year, and are now in hospital suffering from tuberculosis. They get no pension or allowance, although they do get treatment. I realize that a number of these men are receiving hospital treatment as well as compassionate allowances.
I have made inquiries about this matter; I have seen Doctor Kincaid, who is in charge of tuberculosis in the provincial government at Victoria. He is an authority on this subject, and he advises me that there is very little excuse for this disease not being determined at the time of enlistment. He says that science has gone far enough that we can determine this pretty well. I think we have reached the time when the onus of proving that a man's health has been impaired, that
The Address-Mr. Mayhew

he has contracted tuberculosis on account of military service, should not be his responsibility but should be the other way around; that the government should have to prove to the soldier that he did not contract the disease while away. These boys get their hospitalization. But when they leave they have no money, and they are compelled to go into the labour market and find themselves a job. They can last only a short time, and then they come back into hospital in a worse condition than before. In the meantime they have been a menace to the health of the people in the community. I know that the Minister of Pensions and National Health is sympathetic, and I hope he will bring in some amendments at this session to cover that situation. [DOT]
I wish to say a word about old age pensions. It does seem too bad that these old people, many of whom have helped to lay the corner-stones of this country, have cleared our farms and helped to build our railroads and practically all the institutions we have, should find themselves living to-day on a bare subsistence. Their allowance is not enough in many parts of this dominion to enable them to live in comfort. British Columbia recently made some advances to give these old age pensioners an extra five dollars a month, and I think the old age pensioners in that province are probably as well cared for as in any province, but I suggest to the Minister of Finance and to the government that at this time they should give these 'old people the cost-of-living bonus. There are many others whom I should like to see receiving the old age pension. I have spoken of that before. Every time I have spoken in this house I have expressed my opinion that we should have in this country a compulsory, contributory, all-in pension system.
There is one other point I wish to make, particularly because I see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in his seat. I want to congratulate him upon the speech he made the other day and upon his work as Minister of Agriculture. But I was surprised to learn to-day that his department is not going to give the guarantee which it has formerly given in aid of seed growing in Canada. The people of my district are very much concerned about that. Prior to the beginning of the war most of our seed was grown in the old country and exported to Canada, but at the start of the war the dominion government, in cooperation with the provincial governments, guaranteed a price for certain vegetable seed. I understand that sixty per cent of our vegetable seed is grown in British Columbia, and a good deal of it is grown very close to my own
I Mr. Mayhew.]
home. Our people are concerned about what they are going to do, not particularly about this year's crop, but about the crops of future years. It takes two years to grow this seed. British Columbia thought that this was a matter of national concern and that the dominion government should guarantee the whole subsidy for the growing of seed, but apparently the dominion government is not prepared to do that. I understand that the seed branch at Ottawa sends out men, and when they find a farmer with a suitable piece of land for growing seed they tell him how to go about it and guarantee to take at a guaranteed price, all the seed he produces, but up to date they have never had to buy any of that seed because there has always been a sufficient sale for it without calling upon the dominion government to buy it. I understand that now the dominion government is not going to give that guarantee, but I hope I am wrong.

My time is passing and I want to say a word or two on shipbuilding. In 1940 I advocated in this house a programme of shipbuilding. That programme was not started for nearly a year afterwards. But when it was started it went very much farther and very much faster than we expected it would go. Our province is now building more than double the amount of ships that we expected it would, but still that is not enough. We need merchant ships; we need ships that will convoy them across the seas; we need ships that are going to patrol our coasts; and we have not sufficient of any of these three types of boats. I am going to suggest, and I think it is time, that we consider the advisability of converting some of our man-power and some of our steel into the building of ships. We do not need to go very far from Ottawa to find along the railway tracks quite a quantity of materials which, for lack of shipping, we are unable to ship across the seas. True, Mr. Churchill said that we were gaining; that in spite of all the sinkings we had over a million and a half more tons of shipping now than we had six months ago. But I think we should put shipbuilding first on our programme at this time. We should spend every effort upon it. We have at the present time plants wihch are turning out tanks and munitions. If they had to stop and idle for a time in order to allow the steel they use to be used

The Address-Mr. Mayhew
for shipbuilding, they could readily resume work when more munitions were wanted abroad. I do not see much sense in raising huge crops and manufacturing huge quantities of war materials if we find it difficult to transport them across the water. We should devote our efforts at the present time to building more ships. We also need a good many more boats than we now have for our coastal patrol. Almost daily, I was going to say, but that would be an exaggeration, but every week since I have been here someone has written or wired to me saying "the government is going to take my boat for some other purpose than commercial enterprise."
To be quite frank, without wishing to be too critical of our government, I doubt whether the three departments have yet made up their minds as to how much equipment and how many patrol boats are needed on our coast. They will hand out an order for a couple of boats here and a couple of boats some other place, and our yards are running in a hit-or-miss fashion without any programme. I believe it is time that we asked the government to formulate a programme and I would be failing in my duty as the member for the city of Victoria if I did not say so. We need an adequate coast patrol, because all our dangers are not yet behind us.
In conclusion, I will say a word or two about the income tax situation. I shall not discuss it at any length, because I believe that the Minister of Finance will bring in a change as regards the collection of at least the personal tax, and I hope he will also introduce some change in the matter of collecting the corporation tax. I suppose this will be along the lines of the Ruml plan; I hope it is. There is one suggestion I wish to make to him. At the present time he is collecting twenty per cent of the excess profits tax and treating it as a loan to the government. But the people from whom he is taking it have nothing but their own statement as to how much that is. I suggest to him that he could issue some kind of scrip to show what these people have paid in the way of a tax which will be returnable. A better way of doing it than the way it is done at the present time would be to treat the tax as an interest-free loan from the corporations, to be returned to them upon condition that each corporation, after the war is over, submits to the government a plan of development which will modernize or extend its plant, and which is satisfactory to some regional board established by the government for that purpose. The total amount will be a good many million dollars. It would be the first step toward increasing the amount of labour which will be needed in this country for building or
modernizing industries, and, probably, for operating the plants when they are ready. Think, for example how large an amount would be available in connection with out railways alone. I do not think we want the money to be paid in to the government at the present time merely to go back into our hands. I say this although I happen to be a manufacturer, one of those fellows who apparently are not thought worthy of much respect from some quarters in this house. Nevertheless I do not believe the majority of the people wish this money to go back to the corporations to be split up as a melon among stockholders; they would like to feel that it would be put to work for the good of the country and in particular for the good of the district in which they live.
I should have liked to make some observations in connection with rehabilitation matters, but I have sweated enough about even rising to speak at all to-day, and I would rather end my speech here than adjourn the debate, knowing that I would have to rise in my place again to-morrow.
On motion of Mr. MacKinnon (Kootenay East) the debate was adjourned.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
